cover_highlight: A milestone week — Memorial Day weekend opens with rain and a pulled-pork BBQ at Beth and Matt's, the kids host a sleepover gimbap-and-grandma-pizza night Monday, and a sunny Thursday brings the keys to the new house. The week closes Saturday with celebration pizza in the new kitchen and Jungle's Volcano on the speakers.

days.dinner: BBQ at Beth and Matt's — Pulled Pork and Burgers
days.dinner_description: A hosted Memorial Day weekend BBQ at Beth and Matt's. Pulled pork and burgers are the headliners. We bring a thoughtful side or finishing sauce so the family arrives with something special in hand and a quiet thank-you to the host.
dinner_key_ingredients: our contribution: apple-fennel slaw or finishing sauce
days.dinner_notes: Bring an elevated slaw or finishing sauce. Indoor/covered setup likely given the rain.
days.dinner_nutrition_notes: Heavy on pork and beef; aim for a lighter vegetable-forward lunch.
days.activity_notes: Moderate rain through the afternoon — pack a change of clothes for Elsie and an indoor-friendly toy.
prep_notes: Make the slaw or sauce Saturday night so flavors meld.
Defrost dinner protein for Monday's grandma pizza.
days.album_pairing_rationale: Rainy Sunday hosted dinner calls for warm, smoky soul that fills the kitchen on the drive home, not the BBQ itself.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Cider-Snap Apple Slaw Offering
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Bring a crisp slaw of thin-sliced green cabbage, matchstick Granny Smith apple, carrot, apple cider vinegar, a spoon of Dijon mustard, honey, kosher salt, and a thread of extra-virgin olive oil. Keep it chilled and toss once more right before serving.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Pulled pork and burgers are rich; cold crunch and bright vinegar cut the fat like a clean knife.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Glossy BBQ Butter Sauce
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Bring a small jar of favorite barbecue sauce warmed with apple cider vinegar, smoked paprika, and one tablespoon of unsalted butter whisked in at the end. Label it as a finishing sauce for pulled pork sandwiches.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: The vinegar wakes up sweet sauce, while butter gives it a restaurant gloss and helps it cling to shredded pork.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Sesame Pickle Chip Bowl
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Pack dill pickle chips with toasted sesame seeds and cracked black pepper in a chilled serving bowl. Set them beside the buns so people can build crunch directly into sandwiches.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: A sharp, cold pickle layer keeps barbecue sandwiches from becoming soft-on-soft-on-soft.

dinner_question.dinner: BBQ at Beth & Matt's — pulled pork, burgers, rainy Memorial Day weekend
dinner_question.question: Memorial Day is a time to remember people who served and sacrificed. While we eat with friends tonight, what is one everyday freedom or kindness you feel thankful for — something small enough that we might forget to notice it?
dinner_question.why: Eight-year-olds are ready to move from a holiday as 'a day off' toward the beginning of civic gratitude. Keeping the question concrete — food, friends, safety, a dry place in the rain — helps her build empathy without making the conversation too heavy.

recipe_card.nonna_says: Slice the cabbage thin, honey, because nobody invited a lawn mower to dinner. Whisk the vinegar, ketchup, sugar, hot sauce, salt, and pepper until it tastes sharp and a little sweet. Toss the cabbage and carrot with just enough dressing to shine, then let it sit cold so it relaxes. Pack extra dressing on the side and bring pickles because pulled pork loves crunch. Walk in like you helped, because you did.

days.name: Mon 05/25

days.calendar: Memorial Day · Sleepover with Isla & Evyln
time_constraints: Two-track dinner — kids' gimbap night plus an adult grandma pizza.
days.dinner_description: Two parallel dinners running on the same night. The girls — Elsie, Isla, and Evyln — get an interactive gimbap rolling station with seasoned rice, julienned carrots and cucumber, spinach, egg ribbons, and bulgogi or canned tuna. The adults eat Dan's grandma pizza: a thick, square Sicilian-style pie with crushed San Marzano tomatoes, low-moisture mozzarella, and basil added at the end.
days.dinner_notes: Gimbap is hands-on for the kids — set up a rolling station with mats. Pizza dough should rise on the counter through the afternoon.
days.dinner_nutrition_notes: Gimbap gives the kids fiber, iron from beef, and color. Pizza is a refined-carb evening — balance with greens at lunch.
days.activity_notes: Indoor games, gimbap-rolling competition, family movie. Read Chelsie's Memorial Day story before bed.
prep_notes: Mix pizza dough Monday morning so it has 8 hours to rise.
Cook short-grain rice and cool with rice vinegar before kids arrive.
Julienne carrots and cucumber; blanch spinach.
days.album_pairing_rationale: Three little girls together for a sleepover on a family-themed holiday — Sister Sledge writes the obvious soundtrack and gives the adults something joyful to cook the grandma pizza to.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Glossy Sesame Gimbap Finish
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Season warm short-grain rice with fine salt and toasted sesame oil, then brush the outside of each sliced roll with a whisper-thin coat of toasted sesame oil and shower with sesame seeds just before serving.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Warm rice absorbs seasoning evenly, and the final sesame finish gives the rolls aroma, shine, and a clean first bite.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Dry the Crunchy Fillings
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Pat pickled radish, cucumber sticks, and any cooked spinach completely dry before rolling. Cut every filling into even batons so the kids get one clean snap in each bite instead of a soggy seam.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Moisture is the enemy of tight gimbap; drying the fillings keeps the nori crisp and the roll structural.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Grandma Pizza Fried-Bottom Treatment
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Oil the sheet pan generously with extra-virgin olive oil, press the dough out by hand, layer low-moisture mozzarella first, then spoon tomato sauce over the cheese in stripes. Bake on the lowest rack until the bottom is audibly crisp, then finish the edges with garlic oil and flaky salt.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Cheese under sauce protects the dough, while the oiled pan gives grandma pizza that almost-fried bottom and tender center.

dinner_question.dinner: Gimbap night for the kids during the sleepover with Isla & Evyln
dinner_question.question: Gimbap has lots of different pieces tucked into one roll. When friends sleep over, what helps everyone feel tucked in and included — choosing a game together, taking turns, saving someone a spot, or something else?
dinner_question.why: Sleepovers can bring joy and tiny friendship politics in the same pajamas. This gives Elsie language for inclusion, turn-taking, and group belonging before the evening gets overexcited.

recipe_card.nonna_says: Oil the pan generously and stretch the dough into the corners, then let it rest when it fights you. Scatter low-moisture mozzarella right on the dough so the crust gets that cheesy little armor. Spoon crushed tomatoes over the top in streaks, not a swimming pool, and tuck in fresh basil. Bake hot until the edges are dark gold and the bottom is crisp enough to brag about. Finish with olive oil and more basil, because restraint is for tax forms. Cut squares and let Dan take his victory lap.

days.dinner: Babo Pasta — Egg-Yolk Spinach Tagliatelle with Brown Butter and Parm
days.dinner_description: The family favorite. Homemade egg-yolk and spinach tagliatelle, dressed in nutty brown butter, finished with finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano and torn sage. It's a recipe that earns its weekly spot because every member of the household actually asks for it.
days.dinner_notes: Make the dough in the morning so it rests. Cut tagliatelle right before swim, cook on return.
days.dinner_nutrition_notes: Spinach in the pasta delivers folate and a bit of iron. Add a side salad for fiber and vitamin C.
days.activity_notes: Pack swim bag in the morning; warm towel and snack in the car for the ride home.
prep_notes: Make pasta dough during work-from-home morning block.
Brown butter just before serving so the milk solids stay golden, not burnt.
days.album_pairing_rationale: A favorite pasta deserves a favorite kind of groove. Talking Heads keep the kitchen alert and the cooking rhythmic — perfect for rolling out dough between tasks.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Pasta-Water Brown Butter Emulsion
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Brown the butter until it smells like toasted hazelnuts, then pull the skillet off the heat. Transfer the tagliatelle directly from the pot into the butter with a splash of starchy pasta water, toss hard, and add finely grated aged Parmigiano-Reggiano in small handfuls until glossy.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Starch, fat, and cheese need agitation to become sauce; otherwise you get buttered noodles with cheese clumps, and we are better than that.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Crisped Sage and Parmesan Crumbs
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Before saucing the pasta, fry a few sage leaves in the browning butter until crisp, then set them aside. Toast panko in a spoon of the sage butter with grated Parmigiano-Reggiano and scatter over each bowl.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: The pasta is luxurious and soft; crisp herbs and cheesy crumbs give the bowl a top note and a little architectural crunch.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Lemon Zest at the Finish Line
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Microplane lemon zest over the plated pasta and add one small squeeze of lemon juice only after the sauce is built and off the heat.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Brown butter and egg yolk are deep and round; lemon adds lift without turning the dish sharp.

dinner_question.dinner: Babo Pasta before swim practice at 6pm
dinner_question.question: Babo Pasta is one of our family favorites. If a favorite meal could give you a power-up before swim practice, what power would it give you tonight — courage, speed, calm, silliness, or something totally different?
dinner_question.why: Linking a familiar dinner to a physical challenge helps her see routines as support. At 8, playful metaphors make confidence easier to talk about than a direct 'Are you nervous?' question.

recipe_card.nonna_says: Blanch the spinach, squeeze it dry like it owes you money, then puree it with egg yolks until bright green. Work it into the flour until the dough is smooth, wrap it, and let it rest before you roll thin sheets. Cut tagliatelle, dust it lightly, and boil it only until tender. Brown the butter until it smells nutty and the milk solids go amber, then catch it before it burns. Toss the pasta with brown butter, pasta water, and a snowy handful of parmesan. Serve right away, because fresh pasta waits for nobody and you made something beautiful.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Mayo-Crisp, Lid-Melt Sandwiches
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Spread a thin layer of mayonnaise on the outside of the bread instead of waiting for butter to soften. Cook in a hot skillet over steady medium heat, cover for 60 seconds to melt the cheese fast, then uncover to re-crisp the crust.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Mayonnaise browns evenly and the lid hack melts cheese without adding time — exactly the kind of efficiency Wednesday deserves.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Soup Pot Cream-and-Basil Finish
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Heat the tomato soup as usual, then stir in a splash of heavy cream or whole milk, a pinch of dried basil, and black pepper directly in the pot. No second pan, no ceremony.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: A little dairy softens canned tomato sharpness while basil makes the soup taste intentional in under thirty seconds.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Dunking Sticks, Not Triangles
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Cut each grilled cheese into four narrow sticks and serve beside small bowls of soup so everyone can eat fast without the sandwich collapsing.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Shape is technique: sticks maximize crispy edge and make dinner quicker, cleaner, and more fun before swim.

dinner_question.dinner: Quick grilled cheese and tomato soup between the house walkthrough and Elsie's first swim team night
dinner_question.question: Tonight is your first swim team night — that is a real brave-beginning moment. If future Elsie could send tonight-you one sentence before you jump in, what would she say?
dinner_question.why: First nights can stir pride and butterflies. Inviting her to imagine encouragement from her future self builds self-talk, confidence, and the sense that she can grow into hard new things.

recipe_card.nonna_says: Start the soup first with garlic, tomatoes, broth, and a splash of cream so it can simmer while you build sandwiches. Butter the bread all the way to the corners, honey, dry corners are a character flaw. Use enough cheese to melt, but not so much the sandwich slides around like a bad decision. Cook low and steady until the bread is deep gold and the middle is gooey. Blend the soup smooth, taste for salt, and give it a tiny pinch of sugar if the tomatoes are sharp. Cut the sandwiches into dunkers and dinner is saved.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Dry-Brined, Hard-Seared Pork Chops
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Salt the pork chops at least 30 minutes ahead if possible, pat them bone-dry, and sear in a very hot skillet until deeply browned. Rest them five minutes before slicing against the grain.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Salt seasons through the meat, dryness builds crust, and resting keeps the juices where they belong: inside the pork chop.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Lemon-Dijon Pan Sauce
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: After the chops come out, deglaze the skillet with chicken stock, scrape up the browned bits, whisk in Dijon mustard, a small knob of unsalted butter, lemon juice, and chopped parsley. Spoon lightly over sliced pork.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Fond is free flavor; Dijon and lemon make the sauce celebratory without dragging the plate into heavy gravy territory.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Herby Lemon Couscous Lift
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Fluff the couscous with a fork, then fold in lemon zest, chopped mint or parsley, peas, carrots, and a thread of extra-virgin olive oil right before serving.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Fresh herbs and citrus keep the couscous bright, so the meal feels like a toast to the new house instead of a nap.

dinner_question.dinner: House closing day celebration, with swim at 7pm
dinner_question.question: Today our family officially gets a new house. What is one tiny tradition we should carry into it right away — a first breakfast, a pizza spot, a reading corner, a silly doorway dance, or something only our family would do?
dinner_question.why: A closing is an adult milestone, but traditions let Elsie feel ownership of the transition. She gets to help define what makes the new place feel like 'ours,' not just watch grown-ups sign papers.

recipe_card.nonna_says: Season the pork chops early with salt, pepper, paprika, and a little lemon zest if you have manners. Sear them in a hot skillet until browned, then finish gently so they stay juicy. In another pan, soften carrots in butter or olive oil, add broth, peas, and couscous, then cover it off the heat. Do not boil couscous to death, it is tiny pasta, not punishment. Fluff it with a fork, fold in parsley and lemon, and lay the pork chops on top. Spoon any pan juices over everything and call them family treasure.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Rested Batter, Crisp Butter Edges
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Mix the buttermilk pancake batter only until lumpy, then let it rest for 10 minutes while the sausage cooks. Cook in a thin film of butter so the pancake edges go golden and crisp.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Resting hydrates the flour and relaxed gluten makes tender pancakes; butter in the pan gives the edge a proper diner crunch.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Maple-Pepper Sausage Glaze
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: When the sausage is browned, brush it in the pan with maple syrup, a splash of apple cider vinegar, and cracked black pepper for the final minute only.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Maple loves pork, vinegar keeps it from getting candy-sweet, and black pepper gives breakfast-for-dinner an adult backbone.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Cold Berry Spoon on Hot Pancakes
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Toss berries with a pinch of sugar and lemon juice, then spoon them cold over the hot pancake-and-egg stack at the table.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: The cold fruit against hot pancake, runny yolk, and sausage makes the plate feel composed instead of just stacked.

dinner_question.dinner: Pancakes for dinner after Mom's DC car drop-off, YAT, and swim practice
dinner_question.question: Pancakes for dinner means the day is allowed to be a little upside down. What is one thing that went differently than expected today, and how did you handle it?
dinner_question.why: Busy Fridays can fray everyone. This question normalizes flexibility and helps an 8-year-old notice her own coping skills instead of only remembering what felt rushed.

recipe_card.nonna_says: Brown the sausage first so breakfast has a backbone, then keep it warm. Whisk the dry ingredients in one bowl and the buttermilk, eggs, butter, and vanilla in another. Stir them together only until the flour disappears, because pancake batter is not wallpaper paste. Pour big pancakes, cook until bubbles set, then cut a neat center and drop in an egg. Cover the pan so the white sets while the yolk stays friendly. Serve with sausage on the side and maple syrup where it belongs, which is everywhere.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Stone-Hot Celebration Crust
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Preheat a pizza stone or steel at the oven's highest setting for at least 45 minutes. Stretch room-temperature dough gently, keep toppings restrained, and bake until the rim blisters and the bottom is crisp enough to tap with a fingernail.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Pizza becomes celebratory when the crust has contrast: leoparded edges, tender interior, and a bottom with real structure.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Fresh Burrata After the Bake
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Bake the pizza with low-moisture mozzarella, then tear burrata over the pizza after it comes out of the oven. Let the residual heat soften it for one minute before slicing.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Burrata is a finishing cheese, not a baking cheese; keeping it cool and creamy makes the hot crust feel luxurious.

dinner_elevation_tips.title: Hot Honey, Basil, and Flaky Salt Finish
dinner_elevation_tips.instruction: Finish the hot pizza with torn fresh basil, a thin zigzag of hot honey, flaky sea salt, and a thread of good extra-virgin olive oil. Bring it to the table whole before slicing so it feels like a tiny ceremony.
dinner_elevation_tips.why: Sweet heat, fresh herbs, and salt turn familiar pizza into a celebration without making it fussy.

dinner_question.dinner: New house celebration pizza after YAT 9am-12pm
dinner_question.question: If this celebration pizza could have one topping for every feeling in our family this week, what toppings would be on it — excited pepperoni, tired mushrooms, proud olives, nervous pineapple?
dinner_question.why: After a milestone week, playful naming helps her sort mixed emotions without turning dinner into a serious debrief. It also shows her that big happy events can still include tired or wobbly feelings.

recipe_card.nonna_says: Make the dough the day before if you can, because flavor needs a nap. Stretch it thin but leave a rim, then sauce with a light hand so the crust can crisp. weekly_theme.title: Brave Beginnings, Steady Roots
weekly_theme.description: This week has the shape of a threshold: Memorial Day gratitude, a sleepover, the first splash of swim team, and the official closing on a new house. Elsie may feel proud, silly, tired, clingy, or suddenly very grown-up — sometimes all in the same hour. The quiet parenting thread is to give her little chances to be brave while keeping the family rhythms steady enough that she knows exactly where home is, even as home is changing.

dinner_questions.dinner: BBQ at Beth & Matt's — pulled pork, burgers, rainy Memorial Day weekend
dinner_questions.question: Memorial Day is a time to remember people who served and sacrificed. While we eat with friends tonight, what is one everyday freedom or kindness you feel thankful for — something small enough that we might forget to notice it?
dinner_questions.why: Eight-year-olds are ready to move from a holiday as 'a day off' toward the beginning of civic gratitude. Keeping the question concrete — food, friends, safety, a dry place in the rain — helps her build empathy without making the conversation too heavy.

dinner_questions.why: Sleepovers can bring joy and tiny friendship politics in the same pajamas. This gives Elsie language for inclusion, turn-taking, and group belonging before the evening gets overexcited.

dinner_questions.dinner: Babo Pasta before swim practice at 6pm
dinner_questions.question: Babo Pasta is one of our family favorites. If a favorite meal could give you a power-up before swim practice, what power would it give you tonight — courage, speed, calm, silliness, or something totally different?
dinner_questions.why: Linking a familiar dinner to a physical challenge helps her see routines as support. At 8, playful metaphors make confidence easier to talk about than a direct 'Are you nervous?' question.

dinner_questions.why: First nights can stir pride and butterflies. Inviting her to imagine encouragement from her future self builds self-talk, confidence, and the sense that she can grow into hard new things.

dinner_questions.dinner: House closing day celebration, with swim at 7pm
dinner_questions.question: Today our family officially gets a new house. What is one tiny tradition we should carry into it right away — a first breakfast, a pizza spot, a reading corner, a silly doorway dance, or something only our family would do?
dinner_questions.why: A closing is an adult milestone, but traditions let Elsie feel ownership of the transition. She gets to help define what makes the new place feel like 'ours,' not just watch grown-ups sign papers.

dinner_questions.dinner: Pancakes for dinner after Mom's DC car drop-off, YAT, and swim practice
dinner_questions.question: Pancakes for dinner means the day is allowed to be a little upside down. What is one thing that went differently than expected today, and how did you handle it?
dinner_questions.why: Busy Fridays can fray everyone. This question normalizes flexibility and helps an 8-year-old notice her own coping skills instead of only remembering what felt rushed.

dinner_questions.dinner: New house celebration pizza after YAT 9am-12pm

dinner_questions.why: After a milestone week, playful naming helps her sort mixed emotions without turning dinner into a serious debrief. It also shows her that big happy events can still include tired or wobbly feelings.

nudges.title: Give the New House a Kid-Sized Beginning
nudges.context: Closing day can feel huge to adults and oddly abstract to an 8-year-old: papers, keys, logistics, grown-up excitement. Elsie may understand that this is important, but she will likely feel it most through small sensory moments — where her shoes go, which window she likes, what the first snack tastes like in the new kitchen.
nudges.suggestion: Try giving her one tiny ceremony that belongs to her. It can be five minutes: let her choose the first song played in the house, pick the first family photo spot, or decide where a future reading corner might live. The words can be simple: 'This is a big family day, and your ideas belong in this house too.'
how_to: Hand her the key or let her touch the doorknob and say, 'Want to help us officially welcome the house?'
Offer two or three quick choices: first song, first snack spot, first room to wave hello to, or first family photo.
Name what you notice: 'You are really picturing how we could live here. I love seeing your brain make this place ours.'
End with a repeatable line: 'New house, same team.' Use it later when moving details feel chaotic.

nudges.title: Coach the Sleepover Social Weather
nudges.context: A sleepover with two friends is wonderful and also socially complicated. With three children, someone can feel left out fast; with late-night energy, tiny slights can grow dramatic. At 8, Elsie is practicing loyalty, fairness, and how to stay herself in a group.
nudges.suggestion: Before the fun peaks, try a light side-by-side check-in while setting out pajamas or gimbap plates. Keep it casual, not like a lecture. You might say, 'Three-person games can get tricky. If someone feels left out, what is one kind move you can try?' This plants a social tool before she needs it.
how_to: Ask one low-pressure planning question before guests arrive or while food is being set out.
Brainstorm two rescue moves together: invite someone to choose the next game, switch partners, or make a three-person job.
If drama appears, start with feelings: 'Oof, it feels bad to be the one not picked.' Then ask, 'What would help everyone rejoin?'
The next morning, praise one specific social choice you saw: 'I noticed you made room for both friends on the couch. That was generous hosting.'

nudges.title: Turn Swim Butterflies Into a Brave Script
nudges.context: Starting swim team gives Elsie a fresh arena for competence: new coaches, new kids, new rules, and the body-in-motion courage of getting in the water when people are watching. Even active children can feel self-conscious when a familiar skill becomes a team skill.
nudges.suggestion: Try helping her build a tiny script she can carry into the pool. Not a pep talk — just a phrase she chooses. Something like, 'First lap, then I know more,' or 'I can be new and still belong.' When children help choose the words, the encouragement feels like theirs instead of something pasted on by adults.
how_to: On the drive or while packing her swim bag, ask, 'Do you want a brave sentence for tonight?'
Offer a few options and let her edit them: 'I can try one thing at a time,' 'New things get easier,' or 'My body knows how to learn.'
After practice, ask for one detail instead of a full report: 'What is one thing you know now that you did not know before practice?'
Celebrate effort specifically: 'You got in, listened, and tried. That is how teammates are made.'

recommendation.why: This warm, funny chapter book sits beautifully at the edge of independence: children making friends, exploring a new place, negotiating sibling-style fairness, and finding courage in ordinary summer adventures. recommendation.connection: It pairs well with a week of new-house imagination, swim-team bravery, and sleepover friendship skills. Read a chapter when the moving talk gets too practical; it gives Elsie a story-world where new places become beloved through small discoveries.

parenting_data.parent_reflection: At the end of this threshold week, think of one moment when Elsie showed you who she is becoming — maybe hosting friends, stepping toward the pool, imagining the new house, or recovering after a rushed day. What did she not need you to fix? What did she simply need you to witness? You are carrying a lot this week, too; being a steady witness counts as real parenting.

clusters.theme: The Tool Is Never Neutral About Care
clusters.synthesis: The AI pieces this week are all arguing, from different corners, that tools do not merely save time; they reorganize responsibility. Google’s Antigravity backlash is the warning label: if an interface is buggy, confusing, or greedy for tokens, intelligence behind it will not rescue the experience. Felix Rieseberg’s Claude walkthrough offers the happier version, where a floor plan, old receipts, and a $20 hardware button turn a move into something playful and tractable. Dan Shipper pushes the same thought into the workplace: more automation does not mean fewer humans, but more human judgment placed at the edges of agents, workflows, and shared Slack-like super-agents. Gergely Orosz and Elin Nilsson supply the necessary cold water: AI amplifies the culture it enters, including bad code review, weak mentorship, and management’s appetite for velocity over quality. The through-line is not anti-AI; it is anti-magical-thinking. A family closing on a house this week knows this intuitively: the best tool is the one that makes care easier to repeat, not the one that creates new messes faster than anyone can understand them.
clusters.what_this_means: Use AI and systems this week as moving-day scaffolding: inventory, checklists, room plans, reminders — but keep a human in charge of what actually matters.

articles.title: The Pulse: Antigravity 2.0 takes ‘IDE’ out of its new IDE
articles.one_liner: A brief but telling signal that even powerful AI products lose trust when the surrounding experience feels chaotic.
articles.author: Gergely Orosz
articles.summary: The Pulse item is thin because the post is mostly paywalled, but the visible premise is useful: Google’s redesigned Antigravity 2.0 is meeting negative feedback for bugs, poor UX, model support issues, and excessive Gemini token use. The important lesson is less about one IDE than about the fragility of trust in AI tooling. Builders will forgive model limits faster than they forgive a product that makes them feel out of control.
articles.notable_quote: Feedback about the redesigned IDE is overwhelmingly negative due to bugs, poor UX and model support, and eating through Gemini tokens.

articles.title: AI’s impact on software engineers in 2026: key trends, Part 2
articles.one_liner: A survey-driven warning that AI magnifies engineering culture instead of magically repairing it.
articles.author: Gergely Orosz and Elin Nilsson
articles.summary: Orosz and Nilsson’s subscriber survey finds AI adoption full of contradictions: some engineers get more flow, others more context switching; some teams ship faster, others drown in review burden and low-quality code. The strongest finding is that AI works best where guardrails already exist — tests, documentation, code ownership, and senior judgment. Junior engineers may be especially exposed, using more tokens while getting fewer growth tasks because seniors now delegate to agents instead of people.
articles.notable_quote: AI is an amplifier, not a fixer. Good software engineering practices get multiplied. So do the bad ones.

articles.title: 🎙️ How I AI: How the engineer behind Claude Cowork actually uses Claude Cowork & What launched at Google I/O 2026
articles.one_liner: A two-part tour of practical AI habits and Google’s I/O launches, with the best insight being that adoption is often psychological before it is technical.
articles.author: Lenny Rachitsky / Claire Vo
articles.summary: The issue pairs Felix Rieseberg’s Claude habits with Claire Vo’s Google I/O recap. Felix’s examples — building a 3D floor planner from a 2D house plan, mining email receipts as a personal database, and creating live dashboards — show AI as domestic and operational glue. The Google segment is more mixed: Gemini speed, Antigravity updates, Omni video, Flow, Stitch, and Pomelli all sound promising, but broken or unavailable features make the launch feel ahead of the product.
articles.notable_quote: The gap isn’t technical; it’s psychological.

articles.title: How the engineer behind Claude Cowork actually uses Claude | Felix Rieseberg (Anthropic)
articles.one_liner: A practical demonstration of going one abstraction layer up until the computer finds the tedious work for you.
articles.author: Claire Vo
articles.summary: Felix Rieseberg’s examples make AI feel less like a grand theory and more like a household appliance for invisible cognitive chores. He uses Claude to turn floor plans into interactive house walkthroughs, treat email as an inventory database, maintain live dashboards, and even build a physical approval button. His most transferable move is asking not just how AI can do a task, but how it can discover the task and required data without manual entry.
articles.notable_quote: Go one abstraction layer up, then do it again.

articles.title: The AI paradox: More automation, more humans, more work | Dan Shipper
articles.one_liner: A bullish argument that agents create more coordination work, not a clean escape from human involvement.
articles.author: Lenny Rachitsky
articles.summary: Dan Shipper’s predictions are deliberately provocative: CLIs are over, every company will have a super-agent in Slack, SaaS is not dead, PMs and designers may thrive, and automation is a lie. The real claim is that AI moves work into new containers rather than eliminating it. Humans become orchestrators, product shapers, forward-deployed translators, and reviewers of work built for both people and agents.

clusters.theme: A Home Is a Set of Repeated Invitations
clusters.synthesis: The family and lifestyle pieces are preoccupied with a quieter technology: the ritual. Joanna Goddard’s Rec League post celebrates recommendations as a small social currency, the kind of internet joy that says, “I saw this and thought of you.” Trinity Mouzon Wofford’s favorite-things interview goes deeper, treating a kitchen table, morning candles, and slowed-down travel as ways to build the family culture she did not inherit fully formed. Emily Ley’s end-of-school writing brings the ache: elementary years feel permanent while you are packing lunches and planning classroom parties, then vanish into lockers and middle-school hallways. Her summer posts answer that ache with loose structure — tending lists, reading, outside time, camp surprises, hobbies, screen boundaries — not because childhood can be controlled, but because it can be given shape. This is a useful cluster for a week of Memorial Day, swim team, and a new house closing. A home is not made by the keys on Thursday; it is made by the repeated invitations that follow: sit here, eat with us, go outside, bring a friend, tell me what you found.
clusters.what_this_means: As the new house becomes real, choose one small ritual to start immediately — a candle at breakfast, a lawn-chair hello, a Friday swim-team debrief — so the house begins with a memory attached.

articles.title: The 12 Best Recommendations I’ve Gotten Lately
articles.one_liner: A sponsored recommendations list that doubles as a little manifesto for the joyful, human internet.
articles.author: Joanna Goddard and Kaitlyn Teer

Recommendations become a way to catalog taste and maintain friendship. The piece longs for an internet that feels less like performance and more like passing a good thing across the table.
articles.notable_quote: People are missing a positive, joyful space on the internet to express themselves.

articles.title: How Gorgeous Is This $200 Wedding Dress?
articles.one_liner: A favorite-things interview whose real subject is building family culture through meals, pauses, and repeatable beauty.
articles.author: Joanna Goddard and Kaitlyn Teer
articles.summary: Trinity Mouzon Wofford describes her kitchen table as the heart of the home and treats family meals as an inner-child practice because she did not grow up with them. The details — candles at breakfast, beeswax tapers by the case, slow travel with farmers markets and bookstores — are not lifestyle decoration. They are a thesis about making ordinary life spacious enough for connection.
articles.notable_quote: Whenever I’m feeling most pressed for time, I’ve found that that’s when I so desperately need to sit down to eat.

articles.title: Rules for raising teenage boys, the introvert's paradox, and my favorite jeans of all time!
articles.one_liner: A Sunday scroll that turns Maycember exhaustion into a practical case for loose summer guardrails.
articles.author: Emily Ley
articles.summary: Ley names the seasonal pivot perfectly: the end of Maycember, camp packing, lake weeks, and the temptation for summer to dissolve into screens. Her chosen word is “focused,” not as a productivity command but as a family safeguard. Tending lists — read, get outside, drink water — become a way to let summer breathe without letting it vanish.
articles.notable_quote: A beautiful, fun-filled summer can be wasted in favor of all the screens all around them.

articles.title: A farewell to elementary school
articles.one_liner: A tender reminder that the years of lunchboxes, classroom parties, and tiny sneakers are not as permanent as they feel.
articles.author: Emily Ley
articles.summary: Ley’s farewell to elementary school is powered by the shock of old photos: little bodies, enormous personalities, a red bow, velcro sneakers, a Charlie Brown lunchbox. The piece honors the repetitive labor of early school years — sandwiches, parties, show-and-tell — and then admits the devastating truth that repetition did not make them endless. The transition upstairs to lockers becomes a family rite of passage.
articles.notable_quote: These were actually, in fact, the years that did not last forever.

articles.title: Timeless graduation wisdom, the case for hobbies, and a bubble hem dress I love!
articles.one_liner: A busy end-of-school scroll that keeps returning to the same plea: make room for pursuits that are not merely efficient.
articles.author: Emily Ley
articles.summary: Ley’s earlier Sunday Scroll is a collage of end-of-year emotion: bake sales, pool parties, graduation advice, pool safety, sample-sale vulnerability, dog longevity, and a man teaching his 77-year-old neighbor to cook. The strongest thread is her interest in hobbies as a satisfying-life engine. Needlepoint, baking, cooking, reading, and swimming all resist the flattening pull of screens and schedules.
articles.notable_quote: Hobbies may be the key to a satisfying life.

clusters.theme: Optimism Needs a Place to Land
clusters.synthesis: Packy McCormick’s optimism pieces are almost comically abundant: obesity drugs producing bariatric-level results, artificial eggs hatching chicks, AI attacking an Erdős problem, SpaceX imagining orbital compute, SendCutSend reindustrializing custom manufacturing, Isomorphic raising billions to pursue “solve all disease,” Varda testing space drugs, Cerebras and Fervo reopening the IPO window, and Cowboy Space putting data centers in rocket upper stages. It is tempting to read all this as a single fireworks show of techno-cheer. But the better reading is more demanding: optimism becomes useful only when it lands in institutions, factories, trials, supply chains, review processes, and actual bodies. Rust belongs in this cluster because Alice Ryhl’s story is the craft counterpart to Packy’s exuberance: reliability comes from ownership models, compiler feedback, governance, release discipline, and years of open-source contribution. The future does not arrive because someone names a company Cowboy Space Corporation, though a good story helps capital notice. It arrives when bold quests are paired with boring machinery sturdy enough to survive contact with reality. Memorial Day week is a good time for that distinction: honor the dream, then ask who maintains it.
clusters.what_this_means: Let the big week feel big — holiday, swim team, new keys — but pair every exciting possibility with one grounded next action.

articles.title: Why Rust is different, with Alice Ryhl
articles.one_liner: A craft-centered argument that reliability is designed into systems long before anyone celebrates the output.
articles.author: Gergely Orosz
articles.summary: Alice Ryhl explains Rust as a language of explicitness: ownership, borrowing, null-safety, safe refactoring, Cargo, RFCs, editions, and a governance model without a benevolent dictator. The piece is especially interesting on AI because Rust’s compiler gives agents a high-quality feedback loop, while also tempting users into false fluency. “Once it compiles, it works” is powerful, but only if someone understands why it compiled.
articles.notable_quote: Rust was designed to turn implicit failures into compile errors.

articles.title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #194
articles.one_liner: A maximalist catalog of progress, from retatrutide and artificial eggs to orbital compute and AI-assisted mathematics.
articles.author: Packy McCormick
articles.summary: Dose #194 spans medicine, biology, space, math, and manufacturing: retatrutide’s striking Phase 3 obesity data, Colossal’s artificial eggs, SpaceX’s S-1 and orbital compute plans, an OpenAI model’s verified work on an Erdős problem, and SendCutSend’s raise to scale on-demand fabrication. The essay’s energy is exuberant, but the best examples all move from story to verification: Phase 3 data, healthy chicks, external mathematical review, revenue, factories, and lead-time reduction.
articles.notable_quote: Things are moving fast, and mostly for the better.

articles.title: Cowboy Space Corporation
articles.one_liner: A weird, funny case study in how differentiation turns ambition into something investors and audiences can remember.
articles.author: Packy McCormick
articles.summary: McCormick uses Cowboy Space Corporation — Baiju Bhatt’s rebranded Aetherflux, aiming at rockets whose upper stages become solar-powered data centers — as a case study in the Great Differentiation. The cowboy hats and High Frontier language are intentionally strange, but the strangeness is strategic. In a crowded market, narrative makes an expensive quest legible.
articles.notable_quote: Turning Robinhood money into sci-fi energy and compute moonshots is exactly how you should billionaire.

articles.title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #193
articles.one_liner: A progress roundup where AI drug design, space manufacturing, cancer treatment, IPOs, and orbital data centers all crowd the same stage.
articles.author: Packy McCormick
articles.summary: Dose #193 leads with Isomorphic Labs’ $2.1 billion raise to pursue AI drug design, then moves through Varda and United Therapeutics exploring space-manufactured drugs, daraxonrasib’s progress against pancreatic cancer, Cerebras and Fervo IPO excitement, and Cowboy Space’s data-center rockets. The tone is frothy by design, but beneath the jokes is a serious preference for founders choosing hard quests over easy arbitrage.
articles.notable_quote: Y’all mind if the optimists have another good week?

newsletter_data.reflections: The week’s reading keeps returning to one household-sized truth: possibility is only beautiful when it has a container. AI needs review, rituals need repetition, optimism needs institutions, and a new house needs habits before it can become home. Memorial Day asks the family to remember what others protected; swim team asks Elsie to practice showing up; closing day asks everyone to imagine a future and then label boxes anyway. The practical invitation is to make the invisible systems visible: who checks the list, who welcomes the guest, who notices when the tool is helping, who calls time when the screen has won. The question for the week is simple: what are we excited enough to build, and disciplined enough to maintain?

In this episode

Rust is one of the most admired programming languages around – and also one of the hardest to learn. What makes developers stick with it?

In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer Podcast, I sit down with Alice Ryhl, a software engineer on Google’s Android Rust team, and a core maintainer of Tokio, which is the most widely-used async runtime in Rust.

We discuss what makes Rust different from other languages like TypeScript, Go, and C++, and why so many developers say that “once it compiles, it works.” We go deep into memory safety, ownership, borrowing, unsafe Rust, and Cargo.

We also cover how Rust is governed by RFCs, feature flags, its six-week release cycle, how engineers get paid to work on the language, and also look into how Rust’s use inside the Linux kernel is progressing.

My observations from the conversation with Alice

Here are 12 of my most interesting takeaways from talking with Alice:

1. Open source contributions can open career doors. Alice landed her Google job not by sending in an application, but by spending years answering questions on Rust forums, and contributing to documentation and code. She also became a maintainer of Tokio while a college student. One day, an email arrived in her inbox, asking: “do you want to work on the Android Rust team?”

2. Reliability is the backend pitch for choosing Rust over TypeScript. Alice is adamant that Rust is a backend language and not a TypeScript replacement on the frontend. Rust’s design for minimizing errors and maximizing reliability can make it a better choice than TypeScript on the backend.

3. Rust over C++ for development is a strong choice for avoiding a host of security vulnerabilities. In C++, a trivial off-by-one error in an array can become a massive security vulnerability. In contrast, Rust’s memory safety eliminates an entire class of such bugs, unless you are brave – or foolhardy – enough to use an “unsafe” keyword, that is!

4. Rust was designed to turn implicit failures into compile errors. Where other languages allow you to forget something, Rust makes an omission into a compilation error for things like null checks, uninitialized variables, or error propagation with the ‘?’ character. If you mess something up, it’s almost certain your program will not compile. If it does, at the very least you should see a lint warning. We previously covered how Andrey Breslav, creator of Kotlin, purposely made null safety an important part of Kotlin.

5. The hardest part of learning Rust is not syntax, but data structure design. Alice observes that newcomers reflexively build cyclic object graphs, like a Book object referencing Page objects that refer back to the Book. Such cyclic graphs are possible in Rust, but its ownership model makes this hard, meaning that Rust novices end up battling the compiler. Obvious solutions are to use structs and understand how ownership works in Rust.

6. Refactoring in Rust is safe and easy, thanks to the compiler. Alice: “I change a return type or struct field, then just fix the compiler errors until the compiler stops shouting. And then once I’ve done that, I’ve updated every place I need to update.” Rust’s focus on correctness makes refactoring it more straightforward than dynamically-typed languages and Java-style typed ones are to refactor.

7. Rust may be optimal for AI agents because of the compiler’s high-quality feedback loop. Alice’s refactoring trick of just doing what the compiler says also applies to agents: they can talk to the compiler, be told what to fix, and iterate. Combined with Rust blocking entire bug classes by design, this makes it one of the better languages for agent-generated code.

8. “Editions” allow Rust to make breaking changes without ‘breaking’ anyone’s code. Rust editions (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024) can be mixed freely across crates. A library on the 2021 edition works seamlessly with a binary on the 2024 edition. This is how Rust evolves syntax (like adding async/await as keywords) without forcing an ecosystem-wide migration.

9. Rust’s governance precludes a “benevolent dictator for life”. Unlike with Python and Linux, teams in Rust self-organize and delegate to each other. Tough questions are hashed out at in-person events like ‘Rust All Hands’. It’s a good illustration that open source projects can thrive across different structures.

10. Rust in the Linux kernel has graduated from “experimental.” At December 2025’s Linux Kernel Maintainer Summit, the kernel community agreed Rust is no longer experimental. Combined with US Department of Defense regulations pushing agencies away from non-memory-safe languages, this means we should see more Rust in the Linux kernel and everywhere else, too.

11. AI code review may matter more than AI code generation in safety-critical codebases. The kernel community is experimenting with AI bots that review mailing-list patches. Maintainers reportedly find them impressive, especially for kernel code; an area where quality and reliability has always been more important than quantity. It’s interesting that AI might be helpful as an extra quality gate.

12. Risk of AI-assisted Rust: false fluency. Since Rust’s compiler is so strict, code that compiles can be assumed to be correct. However, Alice describes AI agents adding Rust versions of C build flags with no purpose! She also cautions that junior engineers using AI to learn Rust run the risk of not understanding why the compiler accepts the code they produce.

AI’s impact on software engineers in 2026: key trends, Part 2

Tradeoffs of AI tooling, why adopting AI at company-level is hard, what’s changed in two years, and more. The third and final part of a series analyzing our 2026 AI survey results

Gergely Orosz and Elin Nilsson

May 19, 2026

∙ Paid

249

3

21

Share

Earlier this year, we asked The Pragmatic Engineer subscribers about the AI tools you use, how you use them, and, crucially, what you think of them. We received more than 900 responses, and with this article we conclude our analysis of that data, covering:

- 
Tradeoffs of AI tooling. Positive and negative sentiments, like how AI tools often mean less time spent on tedious, repetitive work, but that it often leads to unrealistic business expectations.

- 
Adopting AI at scale is hard. Companies are struggling to achieve adoption that feels productive at the team and org levels. Our survey finds the benefits of AI heavily depend on the engineering culture that was in place before.

- 
Impact on codebase quality. Codebase quality seems to be decreasing, but management at most places does not care. Meanwhile, maintenance duty is falling upon a shrinking number of engineers who still understand increasingly complex codebases.

- 
Less experienced engineers and AI. For these folks, AI seems to be less helpful and they rack up higher AI token bills. Maybe they need more space to learn, mentorship, and support.

- 
AI tooling ‘addiction’. Using AI agents “feels like a slot machine” encouraging “just one more prompt”-type behavior, while some folks think that the pricing of plans is built in a way to “lure” them to prompt more and more.

- 
Changes since 2024. Fewer devs are negative about AI, but there’s not all that much more positivity. The models have become much higher quality, and better tooling improves trust.

- 
Where are we headed? The concept of code ownership seems to be eroding, and collaboration within teams becomes less important.

Previously in this series, we covered:

- 
AI tooling for software engineers in 2026: a detailed summary of survey responses, covering the most-used AI tools, trends, AI agent usage, company size and usage, and tools engineers love.

- 
The impact of AI on software engineers in 2026: key trends. Part 1. Concerns about mounting AI costs, more engineers hitting usage limits, and AI tools having uneven effects upon different types of engineers

Full subscribers can access a more detailed report.

1. AI tooling tradeoffs

What can be said about the impact of AI tooling on engineers this year? Well, based on the responses that readers sent in to our survey, there are some common patterns:

Code and output tradeoffs

Productivity tradeoffs

Research published two weeks ago (5 May) by Microsoft claims AI expands the pool of people who can do high-value work. Our survey found similar, while MS’s findings are based on Microsoft 365 Copilot chat usage.

“AI used to do more high-value work” Source: Microsoft

Obviously, Microsoft has an interest in showing the benefits of its AI tools, but in this specific area, it’s telling that both studies agree AI does allow devs and non-devs to expand the type of work they do.

Software engineering tradeoffs

With AI tools, their ‘mileage may vary’ among individuals. For example, some respondents told us they can spend much more time in a “flow state” thanks to AI tools, as they don’t have to wait for input from peers, can keep unblocking themselves, and have fewer interruptions.

But others say the opposite: that because they can start so many more tasks in parallel with AI tools, they keep context switching which knocks them out of a flow state!

The positives and negatives of these tools seem dependent on the environment respondents work in, individuals’ personality traits, and where users are on the AI learning curve.

2. Adopting AI at scale is hard

One pattern in the responses is that adopting AI at company-scale remains challenging, including:

- 
Costs: a growing concern covered in depth in Part 1

- 
Usage: getting people to use AI tools continuously is not always straightforward

- 
Onboarding and education: at larger companies, there needs to be support to help devs make the most of the tools

- 
Reviewing AI-generated output: code review is a particular pain point

- 
Integrating with internal systems: AI tools are more helpful when they are seamlessly integrated with internal systems, hence why many larger companies use in-house, deeply embedded coding agents

Adopting AI at company-level doesn’t lead to a magical fix for engineering problems, while the benefits of AI in an organizational sense seem to depend on what was in place before.

Case in point, AI seems to amplify pre-existing engineering culture. AI doesn’t change the underlying quality of an organization’s engineering culture. Teams with strong engineering practices get more positive benefits out of AI than those without. Teams that see benefits from AI tools already had:

- 
Guardrails: testing and automation around the codebase and deployments

- 
Documentation: they recorded their architectural decisions and engineering practices

- 
A quality codebase: AI agents will replicate patterns already in a codebase

A few quotes on this from respondents to our survey:

“AI is an amplifier, not a fixer. Good software engineering practices get multiplied. So do the bad ones. Embedding this properly in teams is exciting and important”. – Staff+ engineer at a large company in Europe

“I feel like AI allows both faster prototyping and increased velocity on iterations to production software; it relies on existing best practices / project templates our team already have”. – Solutions Architect at a small company in the US

A workflow that makes one dev “10x” more productive may not work for another. This is another reason why rolling out AI tools doesn’t seem to magically make everyone more productive. A senior engineer working at a large company in Canada told us:

“It feels like AI workflows are very idiosyncratic in that some people derive (I hate this framing, but…) 10x more productivity benefit from them than other apparently equally clever, educated, and diligent developers. It feels like finding a workflow that clicks with your own habits and heuristics is more important than finding a global optimum for everyone”.

AI amplifies individuals differently, so the team impact is messy to figure out. A US-based principal engineer at a large company reflected on feeling disconnected from colleagues because of how they use AI differently:

“I use AI in what I think is probably a more sophisticated way than most of my colleagues, so there can be a disconnect between my work and theirs, which is not good news because I am “The Principal” on the team”.

“The tool that works for you” approach can lead to tooling chaos, even at a team level. While it’s empowering to allow devs to choose the AI tools they feel are the most helpful, over time it becomes chaotic when teams can choose their own tech stacks, and when at large companies there are dozens of different technologies. A staff+ engineer at a 200-person business in the Middle East wrote in their response:

“We’re still trying to figure out how to deal with tooling consistency on a team level. It’s one of our biggest struggles, but possibly more due to company structure than anything else. Everyone is using different tools with little coherence. It’s been rough.”

Some companies have briefly rolled back AI to deal with the negative effects first. From an engineering lead at a 10,000+ person company in Europe:

“Since the AI boom, the quality of technical writing and reasoning from senior engineers in my org has significantly deteriorated. There’s an overwhelming volume of low-quality work product that is generated entirely or in part by AI, which has made it very difficult to conduct meaningful review of RFCs or code. We’ve also seen costly production incidents caused by code written and/or approved by AI, and – while my employer initially bought heavily into the hype – we have now rolled back some of our AI tools to deal with the drop in quality.”

3. Impact on codebase quality

A concrete pattern in our survey data is that codebase quality is decreasing due to AI. The contributing factors are not surprising:

- 
“AI slop”: more low-quality code generated, such as duplicated, verbose code, and poor abstractions

- 
Too many code reviews, which means review quality slips

- 
More bugs: due to faster code output and less strict reviews, more bugs sneak into codebases

We discuss the degradation of products and codebases in a recent deepdive, Are AI agents actually slowing us down?

One CTO at a European startup lists their negatives about increased AI usage:

- 
“A lot of tiny bugs and low code quality if you are not careful, verify carefully, and have good structure and guardrails

- 
AI agents generate too much and repetitive code, making systems harder to maintain

- 
Developers lose understanding of the codebase and become numb to bad architecture and bad developer experience”

According to our survey, management often seems unfazed by decreasing quality, and instead focuses on the higher output. A principal DevOps engineer at a large European company said:

“In our company, we hand AI tools to inexperienced engineers who can’t distinguish good code from bad code and it’s falling on deaf ears in our leadership. They only seem to care about short to mid-term cost savings.”

The maintenance burden of AI-generated code is falling on the fewer engineers who understand and care. A staff engineer at a European company listed the problems that AI-generated code is causing:

- 
“Drive by” contributions are up: many more occasional non-core-engineer contributors adding code but not sharing the maintenance burden

- 
Contributing without adding guardrails: many engineers and most of engineering leadership are not using reasonable guardrails like tests

- 
AI slop from folks who have nothing to do with the codebase: huge volume of slop incoming from people who don’t understand the codebase, but will commit and create PRs without fully understanding what they’re doing

- 
Complexity is exploding: thanks to the above

The maintenance budget is falling upon fewer devs, while the task of refactoring bloated codebases and reducing complexity is left to those still sufficiently in touch with the codebase, thereby making the maintenance burden even worse.

But some leaders “get it.” A CEO at a 20-person company told us:

“While AI has made generating code ‘cheaper’, the monitoring and maintenance worry me; the things that have traditionally cost the most in software. We’re increasing the rate of shipping large amounts of code with less understanding and increasing the unpredictability, so how do we work the predictability back on top?”

There is industry pressure on companies to adopt AI tooling and impose its usage upon engineers, driven by a mix of factors:

- 
Seeing actual benefits of AI and hearing that other teams and companies enjoy success with it

- 
Fear of being left behind by competitors, or becoming less relevant

- 
Anxiety about investor interest if a company is seen as not adopting the latest AI tools.

This often leads to:

- 
Top-down mandates to use AI

- 
Expectation of headcount reduction, with smaller teams doing the same amount or more

- 
Management treating AI productivity gains as a baseline rather than a bonus.

One staff engineer at a 10,000-person US company explained it like this:

“AI is part of almost every work conversation. The entire company expects it to increase productivity and reduce the need to hire people. I keep trying to get better at using it and trying to make it more reliable so I can do more. I do worry about the quality of the work and atrophy of certain skills. It’s unclear to me if those skills even matter anymore.”

Pushing AI adoption blindly triggers red flags. Respondents shared what makes them worry about things going south in their workplaces:

- 
Focus on tracking AI usage, but not the quality of the output. This will likely lead to product regressions and unhappy customers

- 
Pushing for universal adoption. Some companies target 50%, 80%, or 100% AI usage for certain tasks, seemingly blind to how some targets can worsen the quality of output, or simply create wasteful usage. See the trend of tokenmaxxing.

- 
A focus on velocity, but without recognition of quality work. Expecting more velocity and output seems to be the baseline, and there is no recognition for work truly well done.

The “move fast and break things” mantra famously championed by Facebook seems widespread across the industry with AI tools. A senior manager working at a large, European-headquartered company told us:

“I see a trend: move fast and break things, and end up breaking things too often. We have to learn to focus on testing and resiliency a lot more, as with AI-driven development we introduce more bugs than before. But the velocity gain is bigger for now”.

Output over quality is leading to the death of code review at some places. As a lead engineer working at a small company summarized:

“We’re at the death of code review. I used to do very deep code reviews where I’d take the time to understand the architecture and organization and provide feedback on maintainability and efficiency. I have no motivation in spending that time to review a giant PR where it’s clear that even the original author didn’t bother to do that”.

4. Less experienced engineers and AI

The first generation of software engineers who have never developed without the help of AI are now entering the industry. Here is a response from a young engineer working at a startup as an intern:

“I have never worked as a developer without AI. Writing this scares me a bit, actually, but it’s the truth!”

But this will be the new reality for those joining the industry. So, what needs to happen to help a new generation of “AI-native” grad engineers grow professionally?

AI is an amplifier which could amplify the lack of experience. A staff engineer in the US at a large company told us:

“Agentic AI is a fascinating mirror. It can code as well as the user who drives it. If that user is a junior engineer, now you have a faster junior engineer. If the user is a staff engineer, now you have a faster staff engineer.

What agentic AI doesn’t do is magically convert a junior engineer into a staff engineer, because the user driving it still needs enough experience to know what a good solution looks like”.

A junior engineer in Australia shares their experience of how frustrating working with AI tools is:

“I think AI agents are great for vibe coding or prototypes where the code quality and functionality doesn’t matter that much. I think it’s also useful for senior engineers who know what they’re doing.

For junior engineers like myself, these AI tools are stressful to use. I don’t have the experience or knowledge to tell AI exactly what to do or quickly confirm its output, so I spend a lot of time on just triple checking and redoing stuff. I’m overall frustrated, but I’m trying to embrace it as we’ve been asked to by the company”.

Less experienced engineers seem to use more AI tokens and rack up higher bills. Several respondents observed this: director-level folks noted that junior engineers are in the top-spender category in their orgs, and it is junior devs who spend tokens on unproductive use cases.

There should be more space for junior folks to grow because they use AI more, one staff engineer respondent said:

“Companies need to give some breathing room to Junior engineers and help them learn and acquire knowledge using AI tools as a booster and not as a replacement”.

Junior folks seem to be delegated fewer opportunities that could help them grow. This is because senior people can turn to AI for tasks, including those which they would have previously delegated to an intern or new grad. A few responses mention this:

“AI allows me to have work done that I would usually delegate to a junior or pay a SaaS for; e.g., writing drafts, summarizing the news. “ DevSecOps lead at a small company, Europe

“I’ve begun to automate any repetitive task that we previously relied on juniors and offshore contractors for.” - Engineering manager, at a large company, US

“I no longer have to delegate work by writing a very long document and briefing a junior engineer.” - Principal engineer, large company, Europe

Why not consider mentoring junior devs in your organization? It’s clear that less experienced engineers are having a rocky start to their careers, so delegating stuff to them instead of to AI could be of high value for newer generations of talent.

5. AI tooling ‘addiction’

It seems that the rapid feedback loops of AI-assisted development create addictive tendencies, and there’s a noteworthy presence of “addiction lingo” in some responses to our survey:

How the engineer behind Claude Cowork actually uses Claude | Felix Rieseberg (Anthropic)

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

-

Felix Rieseberg, the engineering lead for Claude Cowork and Claude Code Desktop at Anthropic, joins Claire to show how he actually uses Claude in his own life and work. In this episode, Felix walks through building a 3D floor planner from a 2D house plan, using email as a personal inventory database, creating live dashboards from connected apps, and hacking together a $20 hardware “Claude buddy.” He also shares his philosophy for getting more out of AI: go one abstraction layer up, let Claude work in the background, and stop assuming computers can’t solve some of the annoying little problems in your life.

Biggest takeaways:

- 
The biggest barrier to AI adoption is people not realizing they can ask AI to solve almost any problem. Felix sees this constantly—the tools are incredibly powerful, but users haven’t built the muscle memory to reach for them. His advice: whenever you’re doing something annoying that doesn’t feel creative, pause and ask yourself if Claude could do it instead. The gap isn’t technical; it’s psychological.

- 
Your email is an untapped gold mine of personal data. Felix used his email to inventory all his furniture when moving houses: every purchase receipt, every confirmation, every dimension. Claude parsed it all and built him a 3D floor planner with his actual furniture. This same principle applies to clothing, medical records, travel history, or any domain where you’ve been emailing receipts and confirmations for years. You already have a structured database—you just need to point Claude at it.

- 
Go one abstraction layer up, then do it again. Felix started manually entering furniture dimensions into his floor planner, then stopped and asked Claude to figure out what furniture he had. Then he went another layer up and told Claude to find the furniture in his emails. This is the key pattern: every time you catch yourself doing tedious work, ask how Claude could do it instead. Then ask how Claude could figure out what to do without your telling it.

- 
Live artifacts are Claude’s answer to keeping your personal dashboards always up-to-date. Unlike static artifacts, live artifacts refresh with real-time data from your connected services—Spotify, Gmail, Calendar, Notion, whatever you’ve authorized. Felix built a personal dashboard that looks like early-2000s software that updates throughout the day. The killer feature: you never have to manually update your pitch deck, your daily briefing, or your personal reports again.

- 
Choose Opus when you don’t know what you’re really asking for. Felix’s heuristic for model selection: use Sonnet when the problem is well-scoped and specific. Reach for Opus when you need Claude to interpret what you actually want, not just what you said. It’s the difference between “make me a floor plan with units” (Sonnet territory) and “help me figure out how to organize my life” (Opus territory). For most tasks, Sonnet is perfectly capable, but when you need that extra layer of problem decomposition, Opus is worth it.

- 
Kids are the best AI users because they aren’t afraid to ask for things. Felix gets videos from parents showing what their kids build with Claude—custom video games with hand-drawn characters, interactive stories, tools that would have required a software engineer just a few years ago. Adults have spent 20 years in a “mind prison” learning what computers can’t do. Unlearning that is the unlock.

- 
When Claude makes mistakes, debug your workflow, not the model. Felix doesn’t curse at Claude (though he notes it’s useful for the team to know when people do). Instead, he asks it: “Here’s what I expected. Can you walk me through where things went differently? How can we prevent this in the future?” Usually the fix isn’t “Claude can’t do this”; it’s “I need to change the prompt, clean up the data source, or set up a dry run.” Treat Claude like a collaborator who needs better instructions, not a tool that’s broken.

What launched at Google I/O 2026 (30-minute day 1 recap)

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

-

- 
ThoughtSpot—Build AI-powered analytics into your product

Claire breaks down the biggest launches from Google I/O 2026—from Gemini 3.5 Flash and Antigravity 2.0 to Google AI Studio, Omni, Flow, Stitch, and Pomelli. In this episode, she tests the tools live, shares what actually works, and explains where Google is catching up, where it may be pulling ahead, and why its launch-to-availability gap is still such a problem for builders.

Biggest takeaways:

- 
Gemini 3.5 Flash rivals leading frontier coding models in Google’s benchmarks while running four times faster. Google positions this as their agentic coding model, optimized for tasks requiring both high reasoning and rapid execution. If the benchmarks hold in practice, this speed advantage could shift the coding agent landscape toward Google’s tools.

- 
Antigravity 2.0 brings Google’s IDE to feature parity with Claude Code and Codex—but it’s playing catch-up. The update includes projects (folder-constrained workspaces), scheduled tasks on Cron, and subagents for specific tasks. The UI looks nearly identical to Codex, and the features match what Anthropic and OpenAI shipped months ago. The advantage is speed: if Gemini 3.5 Flash delivers, developers might choose Antigravity for well-scoped tasks that need to ship fast.

- 
The /grill-me slash command is Antigravity’s aggressive take on Claude Code’s polite clarification tool. Instead of gently asking questions, /grill-me promises to interrogate your requirements and get to the heart of what you’re building. Whether this is actually more hardcore or just clever branding remains to be seen, but it signals Google’s attempt to differentiate on personality.

- 
Google AI Studio now integrates directly with Workspace apps—or it’s supposed to. The promise: build no-code apps that read Sheets, draft Gmails, organize Drive, and see Calendar without setup. Claire couldn’t get it to work during testing. If it delivers, it would capture internal enterprise productivity use cases and personal assistant workflows where Google already owns the data layer.

- 
Omni is Google’s answer to Sora, focused on longer, production-quality video. The model creates 10-second videos (versus Sora’s 6 or 7 seconds), maintains character consistency across edits, and allows conversational editing. Claire tested it by animating her kid’s drawing, and the output was impressive. The real power will be in production workflows where you iterate on the same characters and scenes multiple times.

- 
Flow is Google’s production-grade video editor built on Omni. It lets you define characters, create avatars, and edit videos conversationally while maintaining cinematic quality. The tool targets creators and marketers who need consistent, high-quality video at scale. Claire tried creating an avatar of herself, but the feature failed—a recurring theme throughout I/O announcements.

- 
Stitch and Pomelli are Google’s design and marketing tools. Stitch is like in-browser Figma with streaming design generation, inline AI edits, and code sync. Pomelli creates brand books, campaign assets, and websites from a URL. Both show promise but suffer from “Google slop,” the generic aesthetic of AI-generated design.

- 
Gemini’s multimodal capabilities remain its strongest differentiator. For work involving files, videos, or transformative work across modalities (document to video, image to text), Gemini models excel. Claire uses them for generating blog posts from podcast videos and animating drawings. The 3.5 family continues this strength; for these use cases, Gemini’s multimodal performance is best-in-class.

- 
The biggest problem: half the features don’t actually work yet. Claire encountered broken features, missing integrations, and “coming soon” disclaimers throughout testing. Workspace integration in AI Studio? Couldn’t access it. Avatar creation in Flow? Didn’t work. When you announce features that aren’t ready, people lose patience and stop trusting your roadmap.

Hello! How is your week going? I love this issue and am excited to share :)

Today, we spoke with Trinity Mouzon Wofford who runs the small-but-mighty superfood brand Golde. Her new cookbook, Eating at Home, celebrates everyday meals to enjoy with family — one review called it “a hug of a cookbook.” Trinity lives in the Hudson Valley with her husband and two girls. “Whenever I’m feeling most pressed for time, I’ve found that that’s when I so desperately need to sit down to eat,” says Trinity. “It’s not always convenient, but there’s a spaciousness that comes from taking that pause.”

Here, Trinity shares 12 favorite things, including a $200 wedding dress and lighting candles in the morning…

- 
Cozy spot: Our kitchen table is the heart of our home. I didn’t grow up eating family meals together, so making our table a gathering place is almost like an inner-child practice; it’s something I always wanted in my life. My cookbook is all about enjoying meals as a family.

- 
Morning ritual: People usually light candles in the evening, but when I wake up, I like to light a few on the breakfast table. It creates a soft transition into the day. I order beeswax tapers by the case.

Left: Admiring California redwoods. Right: Walking through the moss garden at the Hakone Museum of Art while visiting relatives in Japan.

- 
Family travel: We recently drove along the coast from Portland, Oregon, to Northern California, and passed some of the most stupendous landscapes we’d ever seen. When traveling with kids, we’ve learned to do the things we would enjoy at home, like visiting farmers markets, bookstores, and parks. That way, our routine doesn’t shift too dramatically. We also slow way down and lower our expectations for what we’ll do and see in a day.

It’s always the Facebook Time Hop photos that get me this time of year. Brady’s last day of kindergarten (he’s now a rising sophomore). Little velcro sneakers. A Charlie Brown lunchbox in hand. I simply cannot handle the photos of these tiny children who are now ‘tweens and teens. 

First day at our school in 2018. K-3 didn’t know what it was in for!

These were the years that felt like they would last forever. 

A billion ham and cheese sandwiches packed. A thousand classroom parties planned. Endless show-and-tell selections. 

These were actually, in fact, the years that did not last forever.

What is it “they” say? The days are long but the years are short. Ugh, time is a thief. 

We spent the bulk of our elementary school years at a small private school in Pensacola, spanning 2018 to 2026. Five repeat classroom teachers (all three kids had them). Multiple repeat enrichment teachers (PE, Christian Ed, art, music, Spanish). Administrators who gave us their cell numbers. Parents of classmates who became our best friends. A school family like no other. I know, because my oldest is in high school, that not every school is like our little school. It’s something special. And we happened upon it by sheer luck.
