Hi friends 👋,

Happy Friday and welcome to our 194th Weekly Dose of Optimism. I’m emailing you from beautiful Utah, where I attended the Abundance Institute Gala last night and got to talk nuclear with Oklo’s Jake DeWitte and General Matter’s Scott Nolan, and where I’ll be spending today at the state’s Operation Gigawatt Conference. 

It’s hard not to feel the optimism in the mountain air. When we started writing the Dose a few years back, nuclear was a controversial dream. Today, we’re heading into the Memorial Day Weekend that kicks off the summer during which multiple new reactors will go critical for the first time. 

Plus, you’re about to read one of the most action-packed Doses in Dose history.

Things are moving fast, and mostly for the better. Happy Memorial Day Weekend, y’all. 

Today’s Weekly Dose if brought to you by… Lightwork

It turns out, my house has been making me worse at writing. Sorry about that. I have it under control now. 

Lightwork came by my place recently and tested our air and water quality, light sources, likelihood of mold, electromagnetic exposure (turns out electromagnetism does run the world), and household products. It was an awesome experience. I learned a lot, including that my home’s air quality and lighting were undermining my energy levels, our shower water was full of VOCs whose vapor I was inhaling, and a whole lot more.

Lightwork’s assessments are concierge evaluations where they test every aspect of your home that could be impacting your health, produce a science-backed, in-depth report on all their findings, and then help you fix all the issues they uncover. I recommend them. Check them out!

Book a Free Consultation Today

(1) Retatrutide Stuns In Phase 3 Obesity Trial

Eli Lily

Yesterday morning, Eli Lilly reported topline results from TRIUMPH-1, the Phase 3 trial for retatrutide in adults with obesity and at least one weight-related comorbidity. Here’s a summary of the results from Superpower founder and peptide enthusiast Max Marchione:

- 
28.3% bodyweight lost on 12mg over 80 weeks

- 
70.3 pounds on avg. or 31.9 kg

- 
45.3% of patients hit 30%+ weight loss (this is bariatric surgery territory)

- 
30.3% weight loss (85 lbs) at 104 weeks in higher-BMI patients

- 
65.3% of 12mg patients dropped below the obesity BMI threshold

- 
19% loss on 4mg over 80 weeks (47.2 lbs) with fewer dropouts than placebo (4.1% vs 4.9%)

- 
significant drops in blood pressure, triglycerides, non-HDL cholesterol, waist circumference, and hsCRP

- 
no cardiac or liver signals

These are bariatric surgery results in a shot, with a bunch of freebies thrown in. 

People have been excited about reta on social media for a while, but it’s still gray market, so this is a key step towards getting it to the general public, and just an astonishing set of results. People are losing 28.3% of their bodyweight, or 70 pounds, in less than two years! 

For context, Zepbound (tirzepatide) tops out around 20-22% weight loss in its big trials, and the previous-generation Wegovy (semaglutide) at around 15%.

Retatrutide is the first triple hormone receptor agonist (GIP + GLP-1 + glucagon). We previewed this back in Dose #175, in our piece on grey-market peptides and Gen3 GLP-1/GIP/glucagon agonists. The author of the essay we covered, Not for Human Consumption, called these drugs “the holy grail of weight loss medications” before any of them had a Phase 3 readout. Now one of them does. 

This is Lebron-level. Unbelievably hyped out of the gate, and then exceeds the hype.

As with all of these miracle drugs, there are positive side effects beyond weight loss. Retatrutide reduced osteoarthritis knee pain by an average of 75.8%, with more than 1 in 8 patients reporting they were completely free of knee pain at the end of the trial. LDL cholesterol dropped 20%. 72% of prediabetic participants returned to normal blood sugar levels. Seven more Phase 3 readouts are expected this year, including diabetes, sleep apnea, chronic back pain, and cardiorenal outcomes.

Get ready to get hot and healthy. It’s Reta Summer (in 2027).

(2) Colossal Biosciences Hatches Chick From Artificial Eggs

“Before we named the stars, before we mapped the atom, we asked ourselves an impossible question: which came first, the chicken or the egg?” 

On Monday, Ben Lamm's Colossal Biosciences announced that it has hatched 26 healthy chicks from a fully artificial egg, an oval printed shell coated in an oxygen-permeable membrane that lets an embryo develop from poured-in yolk to pipping bird, without a biological eggshell. Researchers crack a freshly laid fertilized egg, pour the contents into the artificial shell (Colossal adds ground-up calcium back in, because the embryo eats the shell as it grows), and watch through the top window as eyes form, vasculature spreads, and, 18 days later, a chick taps its way out.

Real scientists will tell you (and MIT Tech Review's Antonio Regalado dutifully did) that growing birds outside the shell isn't new. A Japanese group hatched quail in 1998. Katsuya Obara hatched chickens under transparent plastic film in 2024. Colossal's marketing is, per Regalado, "pure Hollywood." Which is kind of fair but too clucking cynical. 

Colossal’s real engineering advance is the membrane, which lets the embryo pull enough oxygen from ambient air that the system doesn't need supplemental gas. Previous shell-less methods did, and chicks tended to die. I like the version in which the chicks live, Regalado. 

While this experiment was on a chicken, we have plenty of those. Colossal likes to de-extinct. Its stated goal is the 12-foot, 500-pound South Island giant moa, which laid four-liter eggs no living bird is large enough to surrogate. Colossal staff are reportedly already calling the prototype scaled-up version the "salad spinner." More immediately, the artificial egg is a tool for genetic rescue of endangered birds and, as per our discussion in Dose #186 with not boring capital portfolio company Neion Bio, a substrate for transgenic chickens producing therapeutic proteins in egg whites at a fraction of mammalian cell culture costs.

This is the first member of what Colossal calls its "exogenous development" family. Up next: artificial wombs for marsupials.

With this chicken breakthrough, it feels like humans have crossed a road. 

(3) SpaceX Launches S-1

For the entirety of its existence, human civilization has lived on a single celestial body: Earth. The current paradigm, in which human civilization is confined to one planet, exposes humanity to existential threats that are unpredictable and uncontrollable on a planetary scale. By moving beyond the only home we have ever known, we ensure species-level redundancy and that the light of consciousness will not be tied to a single planet subject to the inevitable hazards of a harsh and vast universe. We do not want humans to have the same fate as dinosaurs.

On Wednesday, SpaeX dropped what may have been the most highly-anticipated S-1 in the history of the planet (until Anthropic files later this year). You can read it here.

Financial highlights include:

- 
Revenue: $4.69B (run-rate ~$19B)

- 
Operating loss: $(1.94B), but Adjusted EBITDA of +$1.13B

- 
Connectivity (Starlink) prints cash: $3.26B revenue, $1.19B operating income in just the first quarter. Its revenue is growing ~50% per year, and profitability is growing faster.

- 
AI is losing money for now…: $818M revenue, $(2.47B) operating loss in Q1. Capex on AI alone was $7.7B in Q1, more than Space ($1.05B) and Connectivity ($1.33B) combined, by far.

- 
But has the monster TAM: AI infra, consumer subscriptions, digital advertising, and enterprise applications - the AI segment - has a company-estimated TAM of $26.5 trillion, which seems small when you consider the size of the universe and the potential to spread Enterprise Applications throughout it. 

SpaceX also disclosed that it’s doing a second compute deal with Anthropic, in which Dario & Co. will pay SpaceX $1.25 billion per month for Colossus 2, which is nearly as much as entire SpaceX makes now. For now, it’s selling compute on earth, but per the S-1, it plans to begin deploying orbital compute in 2028 and scale it to 100 GW of compute launched annually, which would make Colossus seem like a pale blue dot. 

Starlink, which had been the bull case until AI, is at 9,600 satellites, 10.3 million subscribers across 164 countries, and now accounts for ~75% of all active maneuverable satellites in orbit. 

There is no one operating at a higher level than Elon and the SpaceX team, across everything from terrestrial data centers to rockets to satellites to, soon, Terafab. After more than 20 years, it’s awesome to see the company go public (and generate some much-needed DPI for the venture and seven-layer-SPV ecosystems). Is the price a little high? Maybe, yeah, sure. But what would you pay to own a Scarce Asset that catches Statue of Liberty-sized rockets with chopsticks… 

We’ll find out in June. 

In the meanting, after scrapping the launch of Starship v3 last night, SpaceX is giving it another go today. What a way to launch summer. 

(4) GPT 5.5 Pro Makes Breakthrough on Erdős Planar Distance Problem

Take n dots on a piece of paper. How many pairs of dots can sit exactly one unit apart from each other? 

Paul Erdős posed this in 1946, conjectured the answer grows just barely faster than n, and offered cash for a resolution. For 80 years, the best constructions anyone could find were boring square grids, and most of combinatorial geometry treated Erdős's upper bound as essentially right.

This week, an internal general-purpose OpenAI reasoning model produced a proof that disproves it. The model isn’t math-specific, it just thought for a long time and burned an estimated ~$1,000 max worth of tokens, which is pretty affordable for an 80 year old unsolved problem! It found that there's an infinite family of point arrangements that beat the grid, polynomially. Erdős was wrong, and his “favorite problem” is settled.

How’d it pull it off? Instead of more clever geometry, it pulled in algebraic number theory (specifically, infinite class field towers and Golod–Shafarevich theory, of course, why didn’t I think of that) to construct number systems with the right symmetries, then read the geometric configurations off of those. No human had tried this connection. Thomas Bloom thinks it will unlock other long-stuck problems in discrete geometry.

And, importantly, it’s verified. Last October, OpenAI claimed GPT-5 had solved ten Erdős problems; on inspection, it had just surfaced answers from the literature. This time, it got external review by Fields Medalist Tim Gowers and Will Sawin at Princeton, with a companion paper. Gowers's verdict: "if a human had written the paper and submitted it to the Annals of Mathematics, I would have recommended acceptance without any hesitation." It also got endorsements from Noga Alon, Melanie Wood, Arul Shankar. Shankar said the models “are capable of having original ingenious ideas, and then carrying them out to fruition.” The full proof is available as a public PDF.

Ten months ago, frontier models were at IMO-gold level. Really smart high schoolers, basically. Now, they’re doing Annals-worthy novel work. 

I’ve been more skeptical about AI than I normally am about new technologies, and less excited than the average person in tech. Per the evidence that keeps coming out, I’ve been wrong. On the business side and the capabilities side, the pace has been truly remarkable, and I can’t wait to see what problems they’ll solve for us in the years ahead. 

(5) SendCutSend Raises $110M at $1B Valuation 

Jim Belosic (SendCutSend)

Jim Belosic started SendCutSend in 2018 because he couldn't get custom metal parts fast enough for the cars and motorcycles he was restoring. Eight years later, bootstrapped to this point on credit cards, savings, a PayPal loan, and bank-financed machines, the Reno laser-cutting and bending shop is doing roughly $200 million in revenue, growing 100% year over year, and turning into one of the most important on-demand manufacturers in America. 

Austin Vernon's February essay Speed Can Reindustrialize America is the best piece on why the company is so impressive and potentially important. Vernon's argument is that the US is great at high-volume manufacturing and terrible at low-volume, short-lead-time custom work because soft costs (quoting, programming, billing, all the white-collar overhead) swamp the actual fabrication cost on small orders. SendCutSend's whole company is an attack on soft costs: instant quotes, one-click buying, software-routed production. It’s generating ~$275K revenue per employee, and the market would support a hell of a lot of employees. 

Interestingly, Patrick Collison was the one person Vernon thanked for feedback, right above the “Funding Opportunities Apendix.” 

And I guess Collison took it literally, because he reached out to Belosic about investing, and although SCS had never taken outside capital, he decided to take money from the Collisons, Sequoia (Andrew Reed), and Paradigm (Matt Huang) to go bigger, faster. 

Jim and SCS are easy to root for and have become a cult classic over the past few years. Now, the cat’s out of the bag, the money is in the bank, and IT’S TIME TO BUILD.

In other great news for building stuff here, Amca raised $300M at $1B+ from Caffeinated and crew. Amca builds and modernize factories to design and produce critical aerospace and defense components that are supply-constrained and often sole-sourced. 

Jai Malik@jaimalik

I'm excited to announce that @AmcaInc has raised a $300M Series B at a >$1B valuation, led by @caffeinatedcap with major support from @lightspeedvp, @a16z, @Lux_Capital, and others. 

We're on a mission to reconstitute a supply chain that has too often put profit over country.

Now, it can make more of the critical components on which the country runs.

Hi friends 👋 , 

Happy Friday and welcome back to our 193rd Weekly Dose of Optimism. 

The sun is shining, the birds are chirping, Demis is going to solve all disease, Varda is making space drugs, pancreatic cancer keeps getting punched in the mouth, we’re turning whole rocket upper stages into space data centers, and the IPO window is OPEN. Y’all mind if the optimists have another good week? 

Let’s get to it. 

Today’s Weekly Dose is Brought to you by… SimpleClosure

We celebrate ambitious companies every week in the Dose, but ambitious also means long odds, and not every ambitious company ends the same way. Some shut down. Some sell assets. Some get acquired. Some simply reach the point where winding down is the right move.

But however a company ends, there are still final steps to handle: state filings, investor communications, distributions, compliance requirements, asset decisions, and remaining obligations.

SimpleClosure helps founders bring structure to closure, so the process is handled clearly, responsibly, and without becoming another months-long burden.

Whether you’re actively winding down or trying to understand what comes next, SimpleClosure can help.1

Learn More

(1) Isomorphic Labs Raises $2.1 Billion to Solve All Disease

I recently read Sebastian Mallaby’s book on Demis Hassabis and DeepMind, The Infinity Machine, after having already watched the documentary on DeepMind’s development of AlphaFold, The Thinking Game, and a big takeaway for me is that you don’t want to bet against Sir Demis. 

In addition to DeepMind, now part of Google, Demis spun out a bio-focused company called Isomorphic Labs whose mission, right there on the homepage, is to “Solve All Disease.” As of today, they have $2.1 billion more in the anti-disease arsenal thanks to a Series B led by Thrive Capital with participation from Google vehicles Alphabet, GV, and CapitalG, and sovereign vehicles, MGX, Temasek, and the UK’s Sovereign AI Fund. It is the second largest biotech round ever, after Jeff Bezos and Yuri Milner’s AltosLabs came out with $3 billion in 2022.

Back in Dose #180, we covered IsoDDE, Isomorphic Labs’ unified AI drug design engine that crushed AlphaFold 3 on the hardest protein-ligand benchmarks and, in one of the more striking results, rediscovered cereblon’s second binding pocket from sequence alone, an achievement it took human researchers 15 years to confirm experimentally. Our take then was that the engine was real but the proof would come when AI-designed molecules actually entered humans. The money will go towards that, with the first of their wholly-owned drug candidates expected to enter human trials at the end of this year, and to expand the pipeline, continue to improve IsoDDE, and keep hiring the very best talent. 

While there are a number of companies promising to solve drug discovery with AI, Isomorphic Labs seems to have the track record, talent, and war chest to do it. 

Nobel Laureate Sir Demis Hassabis has a history of planning to do things that sounded crazy at the time and then doing them, and the craziest part is that if he does it again this time, the thing that sounds crazy that he will actually pull off is solving all disease. God Save the Queen, and all of us as well. 

(2) Varda and United Therapeutics Testing Space Drugs

Sana Pashankar for Bloomberg

Isomorphic seems promising for Earth Drugs. But what about Space Drugs? 

Way back in June 2023, almost three years ago, I wrote a Deep Dive on not boring capital portfolio company Varda in which we discussed its plans to manufacture drugs in space, where the lack of gravity lets you do things you can’t on earth, and send them back down to earth, where the people who need them are. 

After three years of launches and re-entries with defense customers, the company is igniting stage 2 of the plan: start testing space drug manufacturing. 

This week, it announced a partnership with $25B publicly-traded pharmaceutical company, United Therapuetics, to “explore the use of microgravity in creating drugs for chronic diseases in a deal that could prove out the value of in-space development for the pharmaceutical industry.” 

United makes drugs to treat cancer and high blood pressure in the lungs, and it’s expected that this partnership will start by testing molecular samples of drugs intended to treat lung diseases specifically. 

That’s one big step for Space Drugs, and one potentially giant leap for mankind.

(3) Pancreatic Cancer Just Met Its Match

Ruxandra Teslo for Works in Progress 

Pancreatic cancers surround themselves with a physical barrier that helps them escape immune attack. Adapted from here. PDAC = pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma; TAM = tumor associated macrophage; CAF = cancer associated fibroblast.

Back on earth… it’s been a bad few weeks for pancreatic cancer, which means it’s been a great few weeks for humans. We led off Dose #190 with a pancreatic cancer mRNA vaccine, Dose #191 with pancreatic cancer-detecting AI, and now, Ruxandra Teslo drops a banger on a different pancreatic cancer fighting drug, Revolution Medicines’ daraxonrasib. 

Last month, Revolution shared daraxonrasib’s Phase 3 results. The oral, once-daily pill roughly doubled median survival for metastatic pancreatic cancer, pushing it to 13.2 months. More importantly, it represents a new class of drugs that use a “molecular glue” strategy to hit targets that don’t offer the usual drug-binding pocket. Daraxonrasib targets RAS, a cancer-driving protein found in roughly 25% of human cancers and more than 90% of pancreatic cancers, long considered “undruggable.” This isn’t a cure, but it is a crack, an early sign of the undruggable becoming druggable.

Go read Ruxandra’s excellent essay. Get fucked, cancer. 

(4) AI Chipmaker Cerebras Climbs 68% After Year’s Biggest IPO

Bloomberg

The Information

Do you feel that breeze? That’s the IPO window, baby. It’s wide open. 

Yesterday, fast inference chipmaker Cerebras had a very successful IPO, pricing well above initial range at $185, and then closing 68% above that. Bill Gurley has got to be conflicted… on the one hand, the man hates when a company leaves money on the table in an IPO. On the other, his old firm, Benchmark, is going to make an extraordinary ~$5 billion+ at the $311 opening day closing price. 

Fervo, the geothermal company whose S-1 we covered recently, also IPO’d this week. Its shares popped 33% on Day 1 from its $27 price, and then jumped another 11% today.

Look, things are a little frothy. I’m not buying Cerebras at $311. But we love to see tech companies win, but I’m also just psyched to see some liquidity flow back to LPs to flow back into venture to fund the next batch of companies whose IPOs we’ll cover right here in the Dose in ~8-10 years. 

Plus… 

In older recent tech IPO news, Figma defied the SaaSpocalypse / Anthropic design plugin narrative by crushing its first quarter financial results. The stock popped 8%. Not dead. 

Dylan Field@zoink

Quick update: not dead.

$FIG Q1 results:

→ 46% YoY revenue growth, accelerating for the 2nd straight quarter
→ Net Dollar Retention Rate increased to 139%, our highest rate in over two years
→ Raising 2026 revenue guidance for the year

Design matters more than ever.

(5) Cowboy Space Corp. Gets in the Saddle

Speaking of AI infra exuberance, Robinhood co-founder Baiju Bhatt’s space-based energy company, Aetherflux, has rebranded to Cowboy Space Corp, a company that will, of course, be doing orbital data centers. 

On the one hand, it’s a little 2026 Mad Libs. On the other, though, it kind of rocks. 

Choose Good Quests ✅ - Baiju is Robinhooding himself, stealing his own gains from the fintech app and giving them to the space company. It’s what we want out of our billionaires. 

Also, the idea is pretty interesting. Instead of an upper stage that holds and releases a data center payload, the upper stage is the data center payload. That means that Cowboy has to build its own rockets, in competition with SpaceX, but is focusing fully on orbital data centers by making them half of the rocket. 

Maybe this is a sign that we’re nearing a peak. Maybe it’s exactly what we need to provide AI with all of the compute it will need. I don’t know. 

I think we’re at the point in the cycle where we just sit back, enjoy, crack open a High Life, and root for these crazy Cowboys to wrangle their space GPUs for the benefit of all mankind. Giddy up baby. Yeehaw.

The mystery began on a rainy Sunday with three white paper stars and no explanation.

Chelsie found them tucked under Sharkie's flipper on the kitchen table while rain stitched silver lines down the windows. Beside the stars was a map of Washington, DC, with tiny circles around Arlington National Cemetery, Constitution Avenue, and the long black wall of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial. At the bottom, in Daddio's slanting handwriting, someone had written: Find who remembers.

Mertle, the turtle sock puppet, poked his head out of Chelsie's jacket pocket and blinked his small button eyes at the ceiling the way he did when he was thinking carefully. "Three stars," he said, in his soft voice. "And a quiet day for them to live in."

"What does that mean?" Chelsie asked.

"It means the puzzle isn't loud," Mertle said. "We should match its volume."

Chelsie nodded and tucked Sharkie under her arm. Outside, the rain had gentled into drizzle.

The first circle led only as far as the front porch, where their neighbor Eric was setting a folded flag into a dry spot under the awning. Eric was active duty US Army. Most days he worked in a research lab Chelsie pictured as full of beakers wearing tiny helmets. But Daddio had told her, once, in a careful voice, that before the lab Eric had served three tours in Iraq.

"Excuse me," Chelsie said. "Somebody gave me stars and a map that says find who remembers."

Eric looked at the stars, then at the wet street. He took his time before he answered. "I might know one piece of that," he said. "Memorial Day is the day our country remembers the service members who died while serving. For people in the military, it isn't a long weekend. It's a quieter day, because someone is probably thinking about a friend."

He held the flag a little closer to his chest. "I was deployed to Iraq three times," he said. "Each time, I came home. Some of the people I served with didn't. There are a few names I think about on this weekend. I won't say them out loud — that's mine to carry — but I'll tell you the weekend is complicated for those of us who served. Grateful and heavy at the same time."

Chelsie felt the rain go softer in her ears. She did not know what to say, so she just stood with him for a minute.

"Is it okay to be happy this week?" she finally asked. "We're closing on a new house on Thursday."

Eric smiled, and the smile reached his eyes. "More than okay. The good things — your house, your family, a barbecue, a kid learning to swim — those are some of what people serve to protect. Honoring the day doesn't mean staying sad all of it. It means making room."

He handed her a tiny silver sticker shaped like a microscope. "My Army work is research now. Science can serve, too. Sometimes protecting people looks like a lab."

Chelsie put the sticker on the first paper star.

The second clue smelled like pine needles and wet sidewalk. It led to Ed, who was trimming a maple branch that had drooped after the rain. Ed had served in the Army doing forestry work, which sounded to Chelsie like being a forest detective.

"In the Army, land matters," Ed told her, when she asked. "Trees, trails, maps, camps, weather. If you do not understand the land, you cannot take care of the people moving across it."

Mertle nodded so gently his small head bobbed. "Terrain is a sentence the Earth writes in hills and roots," he said.

Ed laughed — a kind, dry laugh that didn't have any sharp edges. He showed Chelsie how rainwater ran along the curb, carrying little helicopters from the maple tree. "Memorial Day events in DC are part of remembering, too," he said. "At Arlington National Cemetery, people walk between rows and rows of white stones. At the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a wreath is laid for service members whose names we may not know. That matters. Being unknown is not the same as being forgotten."

"That's something my dad would say," Chelsie said.

"It's something a lot of us say, in different words." Ed picked up one of the maple seeds and set it in her palm. "When you remember on purpose, the thing you remember stays alive a little longer."

Chelsie pressed the maple seed to the second star and drew a tiny tree beside it.

By Monday morning, the rain had become drizzle. Daddio packed the map into the car. They watched part of the National Memorial Day Parade near Constitution Avenue, where bands marched and flags lifted in the damp air and veterans waved from open cars. Nobody was silly about it, but nobody was gloomy the whole time either. It felt solemn, which was Chelsie's delicious new word of the day: serious with love folded inside it.

At the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, Chelsie watched people touch names on the black stone. Some left flowers. Some stood without speaking. She did not know any of the names, but she understood they belonged to real people, not just words in a history book. Mertle stayed very still in her pocket, which was his version of standing at attention.

"This is a quiet clue," she whispered.

"The quietest ones often matter most," Mertle answered.

The week kept going the way weeks do. Tuesday brought swim practice and the warm smell of chlorine. Wednesday was the final walkthrough on the new house, and Elsie's first night of swim team, where her arms felt like noodles afterwards. Thursday was the closing — keys, papers, and smiles that almost shook with how big the moment was. By Friday morning, the family had spent its first night in the new house. Chelsie sat at the new kitchen table with the third white star still in her hand. No sticker. No seed. No clue.

She looked up, the way kids do when they're stuck.

That was when she really saw it.

Above the stove, in a simple wooden frame, hung a photograph. Daddio had hung it the night before, before anyone else was awake. It was Dale — Daddio's friend Dale, who worked at Amazon now and who had been deployed to Iraq more times than Chelsie could keep track of. In the picture, Dale was younger, in his desert uniform, squinting a little against bright sun, his arm around two other soldiers whose names Chelsie didn't know.

"Why is that one up here?" she asked Daddio.

He set down his coffee. "It's a picture I like to keep where the family gathers," he said. "It's not about the kitchen, really. It's a way of saying: while we are here, in this warm room, doing ordinary things, people we love stood somewhere far away, for a long time, so we could."

Chelsie looked at the picture more carefully. The two soldiers next to Dale — she didn't know if they came home. She didn't ask. Some questions are heavier than a Friday morning.

"Dale carries them with him," Daddio said quietly, as if he were reading her thinking. "Eric does, too. They both have friends who never made it home. That's part of what they brought back. We can't carry the same weight they do. But we can let that picture watch over us a little. It keeps things in perspective — the time they spent away from their own families, and the people who never got to come home to theirs."

Chelsie sat with that for a long time. Sharkie's flipper was very warm in her hand.

"So the third star isn't for Dale," she said slowly. "It's for the friends he doesn't say out loud."

"That's a good way to think about it," Daddio said.

Chelsie taped the three stars to the wall beside the photograph: Eric's microscope star, Ed's maple-seed star, and the blank star, which she labeled in tiny, careful letters — For Those Who Did Not Come Home.

Mertle, from her pocket, did not say anything clever. He just said, "That's a good place for it."

That evening was the celebration pizza for the new house. The kitchen smelled like dough and basil. Above the stove, the picture watched the way pictures do — without speaking, but never quite silent. Chelsie thought about how a house could be a happy place and a remembering place at the same time. She thought about how solemn was not the opposite of joyful. It was joy with somebody else's grief held gently inside it.

Before bed, she found Daddio in the new living room.

"I figured out the mystery," she said.

"Yeah?" he said. "Who remembers?"

"We do," she said. "On purpose. Out loud when we can. Quiet when we can't. And the people who served carry the rest."

Daddio didn't say anything for a moment. He just put his hand on top of her head, the way he did when words would have been too many.

Outside, the new neighborhood went on being new. Inside, above the stove, Dale and his friends kept watch over a family that was, that night, very lucky to be exactly where it was.
child_wisdom.life_lesson: Memorial Day asks us to enjoy our blessings with gratitude while making room — on purpose — to honor the service members who did not come home and the families and friends who carry their memory.
child_wisdom.discussion_prompt: What does it mean to remember someone you never knew? How can we make room in a happy week to honor the people who didn't come home?

theme.title: Stillness at the Threshold
theme.description: When life gets loud, protect the quiet center that lets you choose well and love well.

anchor_quote.text: Limit your inputs. Make time for signal. Avoid noise.

principles_data.introduction:
Some weeks ask for logistics. This week asks for a spine. There is a barbecue, a sleepover, no-school days, swim practice, a final walkthrough, a closing table, a car handoff in DC, pancakes for dinner, and pizza for the new house. Any one of these would be ordinary. Together, they create that familiar household weather: excitement mixed with fatigue, gratitude mixed with anxiety, joy mixed with the low hum of too many moving parts.

The principle for the week is stillness at the threshold. Not passivity. Not pretending the stakes are small. Stillness is the trained pause between pressure and reaction, the interior room where you remember what kind of people you want to be before the next email, signature, child meltdown, or champagne toast pulls you forward.

Each day looks at one angle: how to enter the week, how not to confuse motion with meaning, how to build a mental model for steadiness, how to carry calm into relationships, how to decide under stakes, how to respect the argument for urgency, and how to make the new house a practice rather than a possession.

daily_entries.title: The Porch Before the Door
daily_entries.essay:
The week begins with paper plates, smoke from a grill, kids running through somebody else's yard, and adults doing that half-listening thing where one ear is on the conversation and the other is already on Wednesday. You are at Beth and Matt's, but part of you is walking through the new house, checking outlets, imagining furniture, calculating risk. That split attention is the first threshold. Before the closing table, before the walkthrough, before anyone hands you keys, you have to decide whether the week will own your nervous system or whether you will own a small part of it. Ryan Holiday gives the simplest opening move in Stillness Is the Key: "Limit your inputs. Make time for signal. Avoid noise" (Holiday, Stillness Is the Key Ch. 2). The point is not to become a monk in a minivan. The point is to stop feeding the fire and then acting surprised that the room is hot. Most family stress does not come from one big fact. It comes from ten facts, seven notifications, three imagined disasters, and a tired body trying to process all of them at once.

Stillness starts before anything dramatic happens. It starts at the barbecue when you choose one real conversation instead of scanning your phone for mortgage math. It starts when you let Elsie see adults enjoying friendship without narrating every adult worry. It starts when you notice that community is not a distraction from responsibility; it is one of the reasons responsibility matters. The house is not the only threshold this week. Elsie is crossing little ones too: sleepovers, swim team, disrupted routines, watching her parents carry excitement and strain. If you want her to learn steadiness, she will not learn it from a lecture. She will learn it from the texture of the day: how you drive, how you answer questions, how you recover when plans shift. The first principle is embarrassingly practical: enter the week slowly enough to notice what is actually here. Noise says the important thing is next. Signal says the important thing is how you meet now. Reflection: What input could you deliberately remove today so the real signal of the week is easier to hear?

daily_entries.title: Do Not Worship the Urgent
daily_entries.essay:
Memorial Day can get crowded in a strange way. The calendar says reflection, service, sacrifice; the house says laundry, snacks, sleepover logistics, and three little girls negotiating fairness like tiny senators. By noon, the urgent has its elbows on the table. Someone needs a towel, someone asks about dinner, someone remembers the thing you forgot, and suddenly the day meant for gratitude becomes another race to keep the machinery humming. This is the common mistake: treating urgency as evidence of importance. Eisenhower, who knew real urgency better than almost anyone, put the distinction cleanly: "What is important is seldom urgent and what is urgent is seldom important" (Eisenhower, quoted in Stephen Covey, The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People Ch. 3). The line survives because it stings. Most of us do not neglect the important because we are bad people. We neglect it because the urgent is louder, more socially demanding, and easier to check off.

The antidote is not ignoring the urgent. Children still need food; guests still need blankets; the dog still needs to go out. The antidote is refusing to let the urgent define the meaning of the day. Memorial Day is a good teacher here because service is often the opposite of drama. Sacrifice is usually someone doing an unglamorous thing at the right time for the sake of people who may never understand the cost. In family life, the scaled-down version looks like making pancakes without resentment, letting the sleepover be a little chaotic, and still creating one minute of remembered gratitude before dessert or bedtime. You do not need a speech. You need a pause strong enough to say, "Today we remember people who gave up ordinary days so others could have them." That sentence can live beside popsicles and wet swimsuits. In fact, it may land better there. The urgent handles the surface of life; the important gives it depth. If this week is going to stay grounded, the question is not, "Did we clear the list?" It is, "Did we protect the meaning inside the list?" Reflection: Where is urgency trying to impersonate importance in your house today?

daily_entries.title: The Space Between Splash and Stroke
daily_entries.essay:
Tuesday has the odd texture of a school day without school. The normal rails are gone, but the evening still has swim practice at 6, which means the day can either drift until everyone is late or become over-managed until everyone is brittle. This is where most parents lose the plot: they try to control the whole pool instead of controlling the lane they are actually swimming in. Viktor Frankl offers the cleanest mental model for the week: "Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response" (Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning Part One). Whether every edition prints the sentence in exactly that form, it captures Frankl's central claim from the camps: human dignity lives in the last inner freedom, the ability to choose one's attitude when conditions are not chosen. That sounds enormous because it is. It is also small enough to use while looking for goggles.

The model is simple: stimulus, space, response. The stimulus is traffic, a missing swimsuit, an anxious thought about closing costs, Elsie asking the same question for the fourth time. The response is the visible thing: sharp tone, calm answer, joke, silence, reset. The space is the only part you can train. Do not romanticize it. Sometimes the space is one breath before you speak. Sometimes it is saying, "I need two minutes," and actually taking them. Sometimes it is noticing that your body is acting as if a swim practice schedule is a charging bear. The power of the model is that it moves dignity back inside your reach. You cannot make this week smooth. You can make your responses less automatic. That matters because children borrow adult nervous systems before they build their own. When Elsie sees you create space, she learns that feelings are weather, not commands. When Dan and Laura give each other space, they keep stress from becoming a contagion. Stillness is not the absence of stimulus; it is the practiced refusal to let stimulus write the script. Reflection: What recurring stimulus this week deserves a larger space before you answer it?

daily_entries.title: Walk Through the House, Not Each Other
daily_entries.essay:
The final walkthrough has a way of making adults weird. You enter with a checklist, a pen, maybe a folder, and suddenly every scuff on a wall feels like a referendum on whether you are competent people making a sane decision. Then the clock keeps moving: 5:30 walkthrough, 7:00 first swim team night, no school because of Eid al-Adha, and a child watching the adults scan rooms with serious faces. This is the relationship test hidden inside a logistical event. Pressure narrows attention. You stop seeing people and start seeing obstacles: the spouse who asks the wrong question, the child who needs reassurance at the worst moment, the agent who moves too fast, the seller who left something odd in the garage. Robert Greene's healthier family-use version of social intelligence starts with this warning: "The deepest principle of Human Nature is the craving to be appreciated" (Greene, The Laws of Human Nature Ch. 2, quoting William James). Under stress, appreciation is usually the first thing we stop giving.

Wednesday's principle is to walk through the house without walking over each other. The checklist matters. The appliances matter. The plumbing matters. But the emotional choreography matters too, because this is one of those days Elsie may remember in fragments: the echo of empty rooms, the adults whispering, the rush to swim, the sense that something big is happening. Stillness in relationships means widening the frame enough to include the person beside you. Ask the practical question, then ask the human one: "What are you noticing?" "What feels exciting?" "What feels scary?" Adults need this as much as children. Dan may process risk by inspecting details; Laura may process meaning by imagining life in the rooms; Elsie may process everything by asking whether her bed will fit. None of these is wrong. They are different bids for safety. If appreciation is the deepest craving, then a tense day becomes easier when each person feels seen before being corrected. The house will become a home through repeated moments of this kind: not perfect agreement, but generous attention under pressure. Reflection: In the busiest hour today, who needs to feel appreciated before they can be helpful?

daily_entries.title: Sign From the Quiet Part of You
daily_entries.essay:
Closing day has its own theater: conference room table, stacks of paper, pens that suddenly feel ceremonial, numbers large enough to make your stomach speak a language your face tries not to translate. At 2:30, the decision becomes physical. You are not merely thinking about buying a house; you are signing your name into a new version of life. The danger on days like this is not fear. Fear is useful data. The danger is letting adrenaline masquerade as wisdom. Ray Dalio's core decision lens is blunt: "Truth — more precisely, an accurate understanding of reality — is the essential foundation for any good outcome" (Dalio, Principles: Life and Work Ch. 1). That sentence is easy to admire and hard to practice when the room is moving, everyone is waiting, and your brain wants either a victory parade or an escape hatch.

So make the lens practical. Before signing, silently separate three things: facts, interpretations, and identity. Facts are the rate, the payment, the inspection status, the cash needed, the legal obligations. Interpretations are "this is exciting," "this is terrifying," "we should have done this sooner," "what if we missed something?" Identity is the story trying to attach itself: "responsible providers," "people in over their heads," "family building a future." Stillness does not erase any of these; it sorts them. You want facts checked by adults, interpretations held lightly, and identity chosen deliberately. The best version of this day is not one where nobody feels nervous. The best version is one where nervousness does not get to drive. Dalio's point about reality is liberating because it says good outcomes begin with seeing clearly, not feeling certain. Certainty is often just anxiety wearing a blazer. Clarity is quieter, slower, and much more useful, especially when everyone else expects performance. It asks: Have we looked directly at the trade-offs? Are we aligned on what this purchase is for? Can we carry this obligation without making it the whole story of the family? Sign, if you sign, from that quiet place. Reflection: What fact, interpretation, and identity story should you separate before today's biggest decision?

daily_entries.title: The Case for a Little Disorder
daily_entries.essay:
Friday looks like the week exhaling through a kazoo. Laura drops a car with a friend in DC. Dan has YAT in the afternoon. Dinner is pancakes, which is either a charming family tradition or an admission that civilization has temporarily lost. After a week of thresholds, the temptation is to clamp down: restore order, tighten the plan, make the house feel controlled before the next surprise appears. The contrarian view deserves respect. Stillness can become rigidity if you use it to sterilize life. Nassim Taleb's great warning in Antifragile is that some systems are harmed by volatility, but others need it: "Some things benefit from shocks; they thrive and grow when exposed to volatility, randomness, disorder, and stressors" (Taleb, Antifragile Ch. 1). Families are not porcelain. They are more like muscles, stories, and immune systems. Too much disorder breaks them; too little makes them fragile.

This is the argument against over-grounding the week: if every disruption is treated as an enemy, Elsie learns that peace depends on conditions behaving. That is a dangerous lesson because conditions rarely behave for long. A little disorder, held well, teaches a better one. Pancakes for dinner after a closing week says, "We can be serious people without making every meal serious." A car errand in DC says, "Community involves inconvenience." A parent with afternoon commitments says, "Adults can carry responsibility and still return to the table." Taleb would call this small, survivable stress. The trick is dosage. You do not invite chaos into the mortgage documents; you do invite play into dinner. You do not wing the walkthrough; you do let the kitchen be sticky for a night. Stillness is the center that makes flexible edges possible. Without a center, disorder becomes collapse. Without flexible edges, order becomes a prison. The goal is not to make the family unshakable by removing all shaking. It is to make the family more alive because it has practiced recovering, laughing, and returning without shame after ordinary messes together again. Reflection: Where would a small, harmless dose of disorder make the family stronger rather than sloppier today?

daily_entries.title: Make the House Vote for You
daily_entries.essay:
Saturday pizza tastes different when it is celebration pizza. The week has moved from smoke at a friend's barbecue to signatures, swim team, errands, pancakes, and now a box on the table that says, in its own greasy way, we crossed something. This is when people usually make the wrong kind of promise. They stand inside a new chapter and announce a new identity too grand to maintain: we will be organized now, calm now, intentional now, the kind of family whose shoes know where to live. James Clear offers a better integration principle in Atomic Habits: "Every action you take is a vote for the type of person you wish to become" (Clear, Atomic Habits Ch. 2). The genius of the line is its modesty. Identity is not a speech. It is a ballot box. You become a family through repeated votes, most of them too small to photograph.

So let the new house begin as a practice, not a performance. Pick tiny votes. The first five minutes after entering become shoes and bags in one place. The first dinner in the new rhythm includes one question everyone answers. The first stressful repair becomes a chance to say, "This is part of caring for a home," instead of, "Why is everything hard?" The first Elsie meltdown in the new space becomes a memory of being helped through feelings, not punished for having them. Sunday's principle returns here: signal over noise. The signal was never the transaction. The signal is the kind of household the transaction makes possible. A home is not built by square footage, paint colors, or the moral superiority of unpacked boxes. It is built by repeated votes for warmth, order, humor, repair, and welcome. Some votes will be missed. Good. That keeps the practice human. The closing did not make you settled; it gave you a place to practice settling. The celebration pizza is not the finish line. It is the first meal in a longer apprenticeship. Reflection: What is one small vote the house should make easy for your family to cast again and again?

source_quote.text: Every action you take is a vote for the type of person you wish to become.
